nodes.name: NF consistency problem
nodes.statement: The consistency of this theory relative to the usual systems of set theory has been an open question since the theory was proposed in 1937, with added urgency after Specker showed in 1954 that NF disproves the Axiom of Choice (see \cite{notac}).
nodes.section: 1.1 Introductory note
nodes.statement_short: Is Quine's New Foundations consistent relative to the usual set theories?

nodes.name: Consistency of New Foundations
nodes.statement: We are presenting an argument for the consistency of Quine's set theory New Foundations (NF) (see \cite{nf}).
nodes.section: 1.1 Introductory note
also_stated_at: In this paper we present a proof that Quine's set theory New Foundations of \cite{nf}, 1937 is consistent.
conclusions: the consistency of Quine's set theory New Foundations (NF)

nodes.name: Jensen's consistency theorem for NFU
nodes.statement: Jensen showed in 1969 that NFU (New Foundations with extensionality weakened to allow urelements) is consistent and in fact consistent with Choice (and also with Infinity and with further strong axioms of infinity) (see \cite{nfu}).
nodes.section: 1.1 Introductory note
also_stated_at: Jensen showed that NFU is consistent and moreover NFU + Infinity + Choice is consistent.
conclusions: NFU (New Foundations with extensionality weakened to allow urelements) is consistent and in fact consistent with Choice

nodes.name: Simple typed theory of sets TST
nodes.statement: TST is a first order multi-sorted theory with sorts (types) indexed by the nonnegative integers.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU
differentia: with sorts (types) indexed by the nonnegative integers

nodes.name: Type of a variable
nodes.statement: The type of a variable $x$ is written ${\tt type}(x)$: this will be a nonnegative integer.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Type-raising map on variables
nodes.statement: We provide a bijection $(x \mapsto x^+)$ from variables to variables of positive type satisfying ${\tt type}(x^+)$ = ${\tt type}(x)+1$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Well-formed atomic equality sentence
nodes.statement: An atomic equality sentence $x=y$ is well-formed iff ${\tt type}(x)={\tt type}(y)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Well-formed atomic membership sentence
nodes.statement: An atomic membership sentence $x \in y$ is well-formed iff ${\tt type}(x)+1 = {\tt type}(y)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Extensionality axioms of TST
nodes.statement: The extensionality axioms are all the well-formed assertions of the shape $(\forall xy:x=y \leftrightarrow (\forall z:z \in x \leftrightarrow z\in y))$. For this to be well typed, the variables $x$ and $y$ must be of the same type, one type higher than the type of $z$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Comprehension axioms of TST
nodes.statement: The comprehension axioms are all the well-formed assertions of the shape $(\exists A:(\forall x:x \in A \leftrightarrow \phi))$, where $\phi$ is any formula in which $A$ does not occur free.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Set abstract notation
nodes.statement: The witness to $(\exists A:(\forall x:x \in A \leftrightarrow \phi))$ is unique by extensionality, and we introduce the notation $\{x:\phi\}$ for this object.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: TSTU (simple type theory with urelements)
nodes.statement: The modification which gives TSTU (the simple type theory of sets with urelements) replaces the extensionality axioms with the formulas of the shape $$(\forall xyw:w \in x \rightarrow (x=y \leftrightarrow (\forall z:z \in x \leftrightarrow z\in y))),$$ allowing many objects with no elements (called atoms or urelements) in each positive type.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU
nodes.statement_short: TSTU weakens TST extensionality to sets with an element, allowing atoms (urelements) in each positive type.

nodes.name: Typed empty set constants
nodes.statement: A technically useful refinement adds a constant $\emptyset^i$ of each positive type $i$ with no elements: we can then address the problem that $\{x^i:\phi\}$ is not necessarily uniquely defined when $\phi$ is uniformly false by defining $\{x^i:\phi\}$ as $\emptyset^{i+1}$ in this case.
nodes.section: 2.1 The simple theory of types TST and TSTU

nodes.name: Type-raised formula
nodes.statement: If $\phi$ is a formula, define $\phi^+$ as the result of replacing every variable $x$ (free and bound) in $\phi$ with $x^+$ (and occurrences of $\emptyset^i$ with $\emptyset^{i+1}$ if this is in use).
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Typical ambiguity

nodes.name: Typical ambiguity of TST
nodes.statement: It should be evident that if $\phi$ is well-formed, so is $\phi^+$, and that if $\phi$ is a theorem, so is $\phi^+$ (the converse is not the case). Further, if we define a mathematical object as a set abstract $\{x:\phi\}$ we have an analogous object $\{x^+:\phi^+\}$ of the next higher type (this process can be iterated).
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Typical ambiguity
assumptions: $\phi$ is well-formed
$\phi$ is a theorem
conclusions: so is $\phi^+$

nodes.name: Ambiguity Scheme
nodes.statement: The axiom scheme asserting $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ for each closed formula $\phi$ is called the Ambiguity Scheme.
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Typical ambiguity

nodes.name: Kemeny's consistency result for TST + Infinity
nodes.statement: It was shown around 1950 (in \cite{kemeny}) that Zermelo set theory proves the consistency of TST with the axiom of infinity; TST + Infinity has the same consistency strength as Zermelo set theory with separation restricted to bounded formulas.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Historical remarks
conclusions: Zermelo set theory proves the consistency of TST with the axiom of infinity
TST + Infinity has the same consistency strength as Zermelo set theory with separation restricted to bounded formulas

nodes.name: Natural numbers in TST
nodes.statement: But further, we can define $\mathbb N$ as $\{n:(\forall I:0 \in I \wedge (\forall x \in I:\sigma(x) \in I) \rightarrow n \in I)\}$, that is, as the intersection of all inductive sets.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST

nodes.name: Axiom of infinity in TST
nodes.statement: The axiom of infinity can be stated as $V \not\in \bigcup \mathbb N$ (where $V= \{x:x=x\}$ is the typically ambiguous symbol for the type $i+1$ set of all type $i$ objects).
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST

nodes.name: Kuratowski pair
nodes.statement: The Kuratowski pair $(x,y) = \{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}$ is of course two types higher than its projections, which must be of the same type.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST

nodes.name: Singleton operation and T operation
nodes.statement: Let $\iota$ be the singleton operation and define $T(|A|)$ as $|\iota``A|$ (this is a very useful operation sending cardinals of a given type to cardinals in the next higher type which seem intuitively to be the same; also, it is clearly injective, so has a (partial) inverse operation $T^{-1}$).
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST

nodes.name: Cantor's theorem in TST
nodes.statement: Note that the form of Cantor's Theorem in TST is not $|A| < |{\cal P}(A)|$, which would be ill-typed, but $|\iota``A|<|{\cal P}(A)|$: a set has fewer unit subsets than subsets.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST
conclusions: $|\iota``A|<|{\cal P}(A)|$

nodes.name: Exponential map in TST
nodes.statement: The exponential map $\exp(|A|) = 2^{|A|}$ is not defined as $|{\cal P}(A)|$, which would be one type too high, but as $T^{-1}(|{\cal P}(A)|)$, the cardinality of a set $X$ such that $|\iota``X| = |{\cal P}(A)|$; notice that this is partial.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Some mathematics in TST

nodes.name: New Foundations (NF)
nodes.statement: NF is the first order unsorted theory with equality and membership as primitive with an axiom of extensionality $(\forall xy:x=y \leftrightarrow (\forall z:z \in x \leftrightarrow z\in y))$ and an axiom of comprehension $(\exists A:(\forall x:x \in A \leftrightarrow \phi))$ for each formula $\phi$ in which $A$ is not free which can be obtained from a formula of TST by dropping all distinctions of type.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
nodes.statement_short: NF: untyped theory with extensionality and comprehension for every formula obtained from a TST formula by erasing types.

nodes.name: Variable translation map
nodes.statement: We give a precise formalization of this idea: provide a bijective map $(x \mapsto x^*)$ from the countable supply of variables (of all types) of TST onto the countable supply of variables of the language of NF.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Translated formula
nodes.statement: Where $\phi$ is a formula of the language of TST, let $\phi^*$ be the formula obtained by replacing every variable $x$, free and bound, in $\phi$ with $x^*$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Comprehension axioms of NF
nodes.statement: For each formula $\phi$ of the language of TST in which $A$ is not free in $\phi^*$ and each variable $x^*$, an axiom of comprehension of NF asserts $(\exists A:(\forall x^*:x^* \in A \leftrightarrow \phi^*))$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Stratification
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be a formula of the language of NF. A function $\sigma$ is a stratification of $\phi$ if it is a (possibly partial) map from variables to non-negative integers such that for each atomic subformula `$x=y$' of $\phi$ we have $\sigma($`$x$'$)=\sigma($`$y$'$)$ and for each atomic subformula `$x \in y$' of $\phi$ we have $\sigma($`$x$'$)+1 = \sigma($`$y$'$)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Stratified formula
nodes.statement: A formula $\phi$ is said to be stratified iff there is a stratification of $\phi$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Stratified comprehension axioms
nodes.statement: Then for each stratified formula $\phi$ of the language of NF and variable $x$ we have an axiom $(\exists A:(\forall x:x \in A \leftrightarrow \phi))$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Stratified formulas are the translated TST formulas
nodes.statement: The stratified formulas are exactly the formulas $\phi^*$ up to renaming of variables.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: The stratified formulas are exactly the formulas $\phi^*$ up to renaming of variables

nodes.name: Set abstract in NF
nodes.statement: For each stratified formula $\phi$, there is a unique witness to $$(\exists A:(\forall x:x \in A \leftrightarrow \phi))$$ (uniqueness follows by extensionality) which we denote by $\{x:\phi\}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Hailperin's finite axiomatization of NF
nodes.statement: It might go some way toward dispelling this impression to note that the stratified comprehension scheme is equivalent to a finite collection of its instances, so the theory can be presented in a way which makes no reference to types at all. This is a result of Hailperin (\cite{hailperin}), refined by others, and discussed in some detail in a subsequent subsection of this section, because it is relevant to the Lean formalization.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: the stratified comprehension scheme is equivalent to a finite collection of its instances

nodes.name: Typed Hailperin axioms axiomatize TST with finitely many templates
nodes.statement: It is also worth noting that the collection of all typed instances of the Hailperin axioms is an axiomatization of TST, not a finite axiomatization, but an axiomatization with finitely many templates.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: the collection of all typed instances of the Hailperin axioms is an axiomatization of TST

nodes.name: NFU (New Foundations with urelements)
nodes.statement: Jensen in \cite{nfu}, 1969 proposed the theory NFU which replaces the extensionality axiom of NF with $$(\forall xyw:w \in x \rightarrow (x=y \leftrightarrow (\forall z:z \in x \leftrightarrow z\in y))),$$ allowing many atoms or urelements.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Specker's ambiguity theorem
nodes.statement: An important theorem of Specker (\cite{ambiguity}, 1962) is that NF is consistent if and only if TST + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: NF is consistent if and only if TST + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent
equivalent_conditions: TST + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent

nodes.name: Specker's ambiguity theorem for NFU
nodes.statement: His method of proof adapts to show that NFU is consistent if and only if TSTU + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: NFU is consistent if and only if TSTU + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent
equivalent_conditions: TSTU + the Ambiguity Scheme is consistent

nodes.name: Specker's disproof of Choice in NF
nodes.statement: In \cite{notac}, 1954, Specker had shown that NF disproves Choice, and so proves Infinity.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU
conclusions: NF disproves Choice, and so proves Infinity

nodes.name: Cantor's paradox in NF(U) is averted
nodes.statement: The apparent vulnerability to the paradox of Cantor is an illusion. Applying Cantor's theorem to the cardinality of the universe in NFU gives $|\iota``V| < |{\cal P}(V)| \leq |V|$ (the last inequality would be an equation in NF), from which we conclude that there are fewer singletons of objects than objects in the universe. The operation $(x \mapsto \{x\})$ is not a set function, and there is every reason to expect it not to be, as its definition is unstratified.
nodes.section: 2.2 New Foundations and NFU

nodes.name: Limit ordinal lambda indexing TTT types
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a limit ordinal. It can be $\omega$ but it does not have to be.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Types of TTT variables
nodes.statement: In the theory TTT (tangled type theory) which we develop, each variable $x$ is supplied with a type ${\tt type}($`$x$'$) <\lambda$; we are provided with countably many distinct variables of each type.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Formula translated along an increasing sequence
nodes.statement: For any formula $\phi$ of the language of TST and any strictly increasing sequence $\{s_i\}_{i \in \mathbb N}$ in $\lambda$, let $\phi^s$ be the formula obtained by replacing each variable of type $i$ with a variable of type $s(i)$. To make this work rigorously, we suppose that we have a bijection from type $i$ variables of the language of TST to type $\alpha$ variables of the language of TTT for each natural number $i$ and ordinal $\alpha<\lambda$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Tangled type theory TTT
nodes.statement: TTT is then the first order theory with types indexed by the ordinals below $\lambda$ whose well-formed atomic sentences `$x=y$' have ${\tt type}($`$x$'$) = {\tt type}($`$y$'$)$ and whose well-formed atomic sentences `$x \in y$' satisfy ${\tt type}($`$x$'$) < {\tt type}($`$y$'$)$, and whose axioms are the sentences $\phi^s$ for each axiom $\phi$ of TST and each strictly increasing sequence $s$ in $\lambda$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU
nodes.genus: first order theory with types indexed by the ordinals below $\lambda$
nodes.statement_short: TTT: types below $\lambda$, membership from any lower to any higher type, axioms all TST axioms translated along increasing type sequences.

nodes.name: TTTU
nodes.statement: TTTU has the same relation to TSTU (with the addition of constants $\emptyset^{\alpha,\beta}$ for each $\alpha<\beta<\lambda$ such that $(\forall x^{\alpha} :x^{\alpha}\not\in \emptyset^{\alpha,\beta})$ is an axiom).
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Weirdness of TTT
nodes.statement: It is important to notice how weird a theory TTT is. This is not cumulative type theory. Each type $\beta$ is being interpreted as a power set of {\em each\/} lower type $\alpha$. Cantor's theorem in the metatheory makes it clear that most of these power set interpretations cannot be honest.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Equiconsistency of TTT and NF
nodes.statement: TTT(U) is consistent iff NF(U) is consistent.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU
conclusions: TTT(U) is consistent iff NF(U) is consistent.

nodes.name: Proof of the equiconsistency of TTT and NF
nodes.statement: Suppose NF(U) is consistent. Let $(M,E)$ be a model of NF(U) (a set $M$ with a membership relation $E$). Implement type $\alpha$ as $M \times \{\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha<\lambda$. Define $E_{\alpha,\beta}$ for $\alpha<\beta$ as $\{((x,\alpha),(y,\beta)):xEy\}$. This gives a model of TTT(U). Empty sets in TTTU present no essential additional difficulties. Suppose TTT(U) is consistent, and so we can assume we are working with a fixed model of TTT(U). Let $\Sigma$ be a finite set of sentences in the language of TST(U). Our first aim is to construct a model of TST(U) in which $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ holds for each sentence $\phi \in \Sigma$. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $n$ be the smallest natural number such that all variables which occur in $\Sigma$ have type less than $n$. We define a partition of the $n$-element subsets of $\lambda$. Each $A \in [\lambda]^n$ is put in a compartment determined by the truth values of the sentences $\phi^s$ in our model of TTT(U), where $\phi \in \Sigma$ and ${\tt rng}(s \restriction \{0,\ldots,n-1\}) = A$: there are no more than $2^{|\Sigma|}$ compartments. By Ramsey's theorem, there is an infinite set $H \subseteq \lambda$ homogeneous for this partition which includes the range of a strictly increasing sequence $h$. \item Any strictly increasing sequence $s$ determines a model of TST(U) in which each type $i$ is implemented as type $s(i)$ of our fixed model of TTT(U) and membership in the derived model of TST(U) of type $i$ objects in type $i+1$ objects is implemented as membership in the fixed model of TTT(U) of type $s(i)$ objects in type $s(i+1)$ objects. \item This model determined in this way by $h$ satisfies $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ for each $\phi \in \Sigma$. This achieves our first aim. \item But this implies by compactness that the full Ambiguity Scheme $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ is consistent with TST(U). We could at this point say that NF(U) is consistent by the 1962 result of Specker (\cite{ambiguity}), but we will continue and indicate how to prove this directly (our second aim). \item We pause to add a useful notion to our logic. The Hilbert symbol is a primitive term construction $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ (same type as $x$) with axiom schemes $(\exists x:\phi) \rightarrow \phi[(\epsilon x:\phi)/x]$ and $(\forall x:\phi \leftrightarrow \psi) \rightarrow (\epsilon x:\phi) = (\epsilon x:\psi)$ which cannot appear in instances of comprehension. We do not define the quantifiers in terms of the Hilbert symbol, because the quantifiers do need to appear in instances of comprehension. \item If we have a model of TST(U) augmented with a Hilbert symbol which satisfies Ambiguity (for all formulas, including those which mention the Hilbert symbol) then we can readily get a model of NF(U), by constructing a term model using the Hilbert symbol in the natural way, then identifying all terms with their type-raised versions (an element of the term model is a class of terms $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in the language of TST(U) which is obtained from a single such term by all possible upward or downward shifts of type by a constant amount: we write this $[(\epsilon x:\phi)]$). \item All statements in the resulting type-free theory can be decided: the truth value of a closed atomic formula $[(\epsilon x:\phi)] \,R\, [(\epsilon y:\psi)]$ in the model of NF(U) is determined by replacing each side of the formula with one of its elements in such a way as to get a well-typed formula, which will always be possible if types are taken high enough, and reading the truth value of the resulting formula from the model of TST(U) with Ambiguity and Hilbert symbol; $R$ is either = or $\in$ [note that the relation interpreting equality in the term model is a nontrivial equivalence relation]. Truth values of more complex statements are determined in standard ways. That this makes axioms of NF(U) true should be clear. \item Now observe that a model of TTT(U) can readily be equipped with a Hilbert symbol if this creates no obligation to add instances of comprehension containing the Hilbert symbol (use a well-ordering of the set implementing each type to interpret a Hilbert symbol $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in that type as the first $x$ such that $\phi$ or as a default object of the appropriate type if there is no such $x$), and the argument in paragraphs (1)--(4) adapts to show consistency of TST(U) plus Ambiguity with the Hilbert symbol. \item We remark that our method of proving (a version of) the Specker ambiguity result is distinctly different from the original method. Strictly speaking, we have only proved Specker's result for TST(U) + Ambiguity + existence of a Hilbert symbol, but that is all we need for our result. \item From this it follows that NF(U) is consistent under the hypothesis that TTT(U) is consistent, which is what was to be shown. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: NF model gives TTT model by copying; conversely Ramsey's theorem and compactness give TST + Ambiguity, then a Hilbert-symbol term model gives NF.

nodes.name: Consistency of NFU
nodes.statement: NFU is consistent.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU
conclusions: NFU is consistent.

nodes.name: Proof of consistency of NFU via a model of TTTU
nodes.statement: It is enough to exhibit a model of TTTU. Represent type $\alpha$ as $V_{\omega+\alpha} \times \{\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha<\lambda$ ($V_{\omega+\alpha}$ being the rank indexed by $\omega+\alpha$ in the usual cumulative hierarchy). Define $\in_{\alpha,\beta}$ for $\alpha<\beta<\lambda$ as $$\{((x,\alpha),(y,\beta)):x \in V_{\omega+\alpha} \wedge y \in V_{\omega+\alpha+1} \wedge x \in y\}.$$ This gives a model of TTTU in which the membership of type $\alpha$ in type $\beta$ is defined in such a way that each $(y,\beta)$ with $y \in V_{\omega+\beta} \setminus V_{\omega+\alpha+1}$ is interpreted as an urelement over type $\alpha$. Our use of $V_{\omega+\alpha}$ enforces Infinity in the resulting models of NFU (note that we did not have to do this: if we set $\lambda=\omega$ and interpret type $\alpha$ using $V_\alpha$ we prove the consistency of NFU with the negation of Infinity). It should be clear that Choice (stated in a stratified way) holds in the models of NFU eventually obtained if it holds in the ambient set theory. This shows in fact that mathematics in NFU is quite ordinary (with respect to stratified sentences), because mathematics in the models of TSTU embedded in the indicated model of TTTU is quite ordinary. The notorious ways in which NF evades the paradoxes of Russell, Cantor and Burali-Forti can be examined in actual models and we can see that they work and how they work (since they work in NFU in the same way they work in NF).
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a TTTU model with types $V_{\omega+\alpha}\times\{\alpha\}$ and urelements above $V_{\omega+\alpha+1}$.

nodes.name: Relation to Jensen's original argument
nodes.statement: Of course Jensen did not phrase his argument in terms of tangled type theory. Our contribution here was to reverse engineer from Jensen's original argument for the consistency of NFU an argument for the consistency of NF itself, which requires additional input which we did not know how to supply (a proof of the consistency of TTT itself). An intuitive way to say what is happening here is that Jensen noticed that it is possible to skip types in a certain sense in TSTU in a way which is not obviously possible in TST itself; to suppose that TTT might be consistent is to suppose that such type skipping is also possible in TST, and the description of TTT is an explicit realization of what is meant by this. We leave it to the historically inclined reader to examine Jensen's original proof and determine the exact relationship between the approaches.

nodes.name: Jensen's alpha-models theorem for NFU
nodes.statement: Jensen proved in \cite{nfu} that for any infinite ordinal $\alpha$ of the metatheory, there is a model of NFU + Infinity in which there is a well-ordering of type $\alpha$.

assumptions: any infinite ordinal $\alpha$ of the metatheory
conclusions: there is a model of NFU + Infinity in which there is a well-ordering of type $\alpha$

nodes.name: Ordinal in the theories
nodes.statement: In any of the theories under discussion, an ordinal is taken to be an equivalence class of well-orderings under similarity.

nodes.name: Implemented ordinal
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is an ordinal of the metatheory, we say that $\alpha$ is {\em implemented\/} in a type of one of the theories under discussion exactly if there is an ordinal in that type (in the sense of the theory) whose elements in fact correspond to well-orderings of order type $\alpha$ in the sense of the metatheory, in the sense outlined in the previous paragraph.

nodes.name: Implementing ordinal contains all well-orderings of that type
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to show that if $\alpha$ is implemented in a type, the ordinal implementing it will contain all well-orderings of appropriate type in the sense of the theory whose order type is $\alpha$ in the sense of the metatheory.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$
assumptions: $\alpha$ is implemented in a type
conclusions: the ordinal implementing it will contain all well-orderings of appropriate type in the sense of the theory whose order type is $\alpha$ in the sense of the metatheory

nodes.name: Existence of alpha-models of NF(U) from TTT(U)
nodes.statement: For any infinite ordinal $\alpha$ of the metatheory, if there is a model of TTT(U) in which the ordinal $\alpha$ has an implementation $\alpha^s$ for each strictly increasing sequence $s$ of types, by which we mean an ordinal in type $s_4$ whose elements of type $s_3$ correspond to well-orderings of order type $\alpha$ of subsets of type $s_0$, using types $s_1$ and $s_2$ for the intermediate pairing machinery, and which is such that the ordinal $\lambda$ indexing the types is a strong limit cardinal of cofinality $>|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$, then there is a model of NF(U) in which the ordinal $\alpha$ is implemented, which further satisfies [after neglect of types] any sentence in the language of TST(U) whose translations via all increasing sequences of types are satisfied in the model of TTT(U).
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$
nodes.statement_short: If a TTT(U) model implements $\alpha$ at every type sequence and $\lambda$ is a strong limit of large cofinality, there is an NF(U) model implementing $\alpha$.
assumptions: there is a model of TTT(U) in which the ordinal $\alpha$ has an implementation $\alpha^s$ for each strictly increasing sequence $s$ of types
the ordinal $\lambda$ indexing the types is a strong limit cardinal of cofinality $>|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$
conclusions: there is a model of NF(U) in which the ordinal $\alpha$ is implemented

nodes.name: Proof of the alpha-models theorem
nodes.statement: The proof is a modified version of the proof given above for consistency of NF(U), using a more powerful partition principle. We do not claim originality, referring the reader to \cite{nfu}, but our presentation is not the same, and it is adapted to talk of tangled type theory. The Erd\H{o}s--Rado theorem tells us that for a natural number $n\geq 1$ and an infinite cardinal $\mu$, any partition of $\exp^n(\mu)$ into $\mu$ compartments has a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$. This is not quite the usual formulation, but easily follows from it. We extend the language of TTT(U) to include constant terms $\alpha^s$ and $\beta^s$ for each ordinal $\beta < \alpha$ of the metatheory for each sequence $s$ as described above. We similarly extend the language of TST(U) (in this case only needing constants $\alpha^i$ and $\beta^i$ for $\beta<\alpha$ for each $i\geq4$), and note that the translation of a sentence of TST(U) with language augmented with these ordinal constants into terms of a strictly increasing sequence of types in TTT(U) is straightforward, and we allow use of these constants in the comprehension axiom of TTT(U) as usual. We further include the Hilbert symbol in our language, with the same restriction stated above that the Hilbert symbol may not appear in instances of comprehension, noting our intention to construct a term model. We consider partitions of $[\lambda]^n$ determined by the set $\Sigma_n$ of {\em all\/} closed Hilbert symbols (``closed" meaning the symbol contains no parameters) of the form $(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i < \alpha^i \wedge \phi)$ in the language of TST(U) augmented as indicated above and using only types less than $n$, with the compartment in the partition containing $A \in [\lambda]^n$ determined by the ordinal values $<\alpha$ [or default value, where we assume the default value is not an ordinal] assigned to all of these terms in our model of TTT(U) when types $0-(n-1)$ are replaced by the types in $A$ in increasing order in each of the Hilbert symbols in $\Sigma_n$. Here we are speaking loosely in that we say an ordinal $\gamma<\alpha$ is assigned as value to $(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i < \alpha^i \wedge \phi)$ when its value is in fact $\gamma^i$: it should be clear that this is unproblematic and easier to say. There are no more than $|\alpha|$ such Hilbert symbols, and no more than $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$ compartments in each of these partitions. Note that assignment of values to all such Hilbert symbols induces a complete assignment of truth values to sentences of the extended language: $$(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i<\alpha \wedge \beta^i<2 \wedge (\beta=1 \leftrightarrow \phi))$$ codes a sentence $\phi$ into $\Sigma_n$ if $\phi$ mentions only types below $n > i$, because the assignment of ordinal value to this term corresponds to the assignment of truth value to $\phi$. The Erd\H{o}s--Rado theorem allows us to conclude that for any infinite $\mu<\lambda$, we have a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$ for the given partition in $\exp^n(\mu)<\lambda$. Further, we can find a single assignment of values to Hilbert symbols as described above which is associated with arbitrarily large homogeneous sets below $\lambda$, because the cofinality of $\lambda$ is greater than $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$, the cardinality of the set of compartments in the partition, corresponding precisely to the cardinality of the set of such assignments of values. If we have chosen such an assignment of values for a specific value of $n$, we can further choose such an assignment of values for $n+1$ which extends it: for any $\mu$, choose a homogeneous set for the partition of $[\lambda]^n$ realizing the fixed assignment of values and of cardinality $\nu > \exp^{n+1}(\mu)$, then find a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$ for the partition of $[\lambda]^{n+1}$ inside this homogeneous set, which will determine an assignment of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types extending the fixed one chosen for Hilbert symbols using $n$ types. Thus there are arbitrarily large homogeneous sets for assignments of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types extending the fixed one for Hilbert symbols using $n$ types. Thus there is a fixed assignment of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types which extends the given fixed assignment for $n$ types and which is associated with arbitrarily large homogeneous sets, by the already stated considerations of cofinality. Thus we can proceed through $\omega$ steps and find an assignment of values to all Hilbert symbols with the property that its restriction to any fixed number $n$ of types is realized in arbitrarily large homogenous sets below $\lambda$. Thus we have constructed a complete assignment of values to such Hilbert symbols in the extended TST(U) language, and thus a complete assignment of truth values to all sentences, which is ambiguous [invariant under displacement of types] and consistent with any statement holding at all sequences of types in the model of TTT(U). Thus for example we will get extensionality if the model of TTTU is actually a model of TTT. In fact, for any fixed $n$ all these assignments for Hilbert symbols mentioning only types less than $n$ will be realized at some sequence of types in the model of TTT(U) [verifying that this assignment of values is consistent and in effect a complete description of a model of NF(U)]. Further, this model of NFU contains no ordinal less than what it calls $\alpha$ other than the ordinals which it calls $\beta$ for $\beta<\alpha$ in the metatheory, and the natural well-ordering on these ordinals is realized in the model of NF(U) and corresponds to a well-ordering of order type $\alpha$ in the metatheory. The reason for this is that the model of NFU is a term model, and any term denoting an ordinal less than $\alpha$ can be slightly modified to the exact form used in defining the partitions, and the process will assign that term a concrete value less than $\alpha$, an actual ordinal $\beta<\alpha$ of the metatheory, so the order on the ordinals $<\alpha$ in the model of NF(U) has order type $\alpha$ in the metatheory.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$
nodes.statement_short: Erdős–Rado partitions of Hilbert-symbol values give a coherent ambiguous assignment over all types, yielding a term model of NF(U) implementing $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Erdős–Rado theorem
nodes.statement: The Erd\H{o}s--Rado theorem tells us that for a natural number $n\geq 1$ and an infinite cardinal $\mu$, any partition of $\exp^n(\mu)$ into $\mu$ compartments has a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$
assumptions: a natural number $n\geq 1$ and an infinite cardinal $\mu$
conclusions: any partition of $\exp^n(\mu)$ into $\mu$ compartments has a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$

nodes.name: extensionality axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\forall y:(\forall z:z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y)\rightarrow x=y))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: anti-intersection axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall xy:(\exists z:(\forall w:w \in z \leftrightarrow \neg(w \in x \wedge w \in y))))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: singleton axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall z:z \in y \leftrightarrow z = x)))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Singleton notation
nodes.statement: $\{x\}$ denotes for each $x$ the set whose only element is $x$, whose existence is provided by the previous axiom.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Iterated singleton operation
nodes.statement: We define $\iota(x)$ as $\{x\}$ and define $\iota^1(x)$ as $\iota(x)$ and $\iota^{n+1}(x)$ as $\{\iota^n(x)\}$, for each concrete natural number $n$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: cardinal one axiom
nodes.statement: $(\exists x:(\forall y:y \in x \leftrightarrow (\exists z:(\forall w:w \in y \leftrightarrow w = z))))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Cardinal one
nodes.statement: We define 1 as the set of all singletons, provided by the previous axiom.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Sheffer stroke of sets
nodes.statement: $x | y$ denotes the set $z$ whose existence is provided by the anti-intersection axiom: $z \in x | y \leftrightarrow \neg(z \in x \wedge z \in y)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Complement
nodes.statement: We define $x^c$ as $x | x$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Intersection
nodes.statement: We define $x \cap y$ as $(x|y)^c$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Union
nodes.statement: We define $x \cup y$ as $x^c | y^c$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Universal set
nodes.statement: We define $V$ as $1|1^c$ (noting that it is straightforward to prove $x|x^c = V$ for any $x$, since this is the universal set).
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Unordered pair
nodes.statement: We define $\{x,y\}$ as $\{x\} \cup \{y\}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Ordered pair
nodes.statement: We define $(x,y)$ as $\{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Ordered triple
nodes.statement: We define $(x,y,z)$ as $(\{\{x\}\},(y,z))$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Ordered n-tuple
nodes.statement: More generally, we define $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ as $(\iota^{2n-4}(x_1),(x_2,\ldots,x_n))$ for $n>2$ a concrete natural number. [The treatment of $n$-tuples is what makes this axiomatization singularly awful].
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: cross product axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall z:z \in y \leftrightarrow (\exists wt:z = (w,t) \wedge t \in x))))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Product with the universe on the left
nodes.statement: We define $V \times x$ as the set introduced by the previous axiom: $z \in V \times x \leftrightarrow (\exists wt:z = (w,t) \wedge t \in x)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: converse axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall zw:(z,w)\in y \leftrightarrow (w,z) \in x)))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Converse relation
nodes.statement: For any set $R$, we define $R^{-1}$ as the intersection of $V \times V$ with a set introduced by the previous axiom: $$(\forall zw:(z,w)\in R^{-1} \leftrightarrow (w,z) \in R) \wedge (\forall u:u \in R^{-1} \rightarrow (\exists zw:(z,w)=u)).$$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Cartesian products
nodes.statement: We define $x \times V$ as $(V \times x)^{-1}$ and $x \times y$ as $(x \times V) \cap (V \times y)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Double singleton image
nodes.statement: We define $\iota^2``x$ as $(x \times x) \cap 1$. This is the image of $x$ under the double singleton operation.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Iterated double singleton image
nodes.statement: Define $\iota^{2(n+1)}``x$ as $\iota^2``(\iota^{2n}``x)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: n-fold cartesian product
nodes.statement: We define $x_1 \times x_2 \ldots \times x_n$ as $\iota^{2(n-2)}``x \times (x_2 \times \ldots \times x_n)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Set of all n-tuples
nodes.statement: We define $V^1$ as $V$ and $V^{n+1}$ as $\iota^{2(n-1)}``V\times V^n$, for each concrete $n$. $V^n$ is the set of all $n$-tuples.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: singleton image axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall zw:(\{z\},\{w\}) \in y \leftrightarrow (z,w) \in x)))$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Singleton image of a relation
nodes.statement: We define $R^{\iota}$ for any set $R$ as the intersection of a set provided by the previous axiom with $1 \times 1$. $R^{\iota}$ is the set whose members are exactly the ordered pairs $(\{z\},\{w\})$ such that $(z,w)\in R$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Iterated singleton image of a relation
nodes.statement: Let $R^{\iota^1}$ be defined as $R^{\iota}$ and $R^{\iota^{n+1}}$ be defined as $(R^{\iota^n})^\iota$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: insertion two axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall zwt:(z,w,t) \in y \leftrightarrow (z,t) \in x)))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Insertion two operation
nodes.statement: We define $I_2(x)$ as the intersection of a set provided by the previous axiom with $V \times V \times V$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: insertion three axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall zwt:(z,w,t) \in y \leftrightarrow (z,w) \in x)))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Insertion three operation
nodes.statement: We define $I_3(x)$ as the intersection of a set provided by the previous axiom with $V \times V \times V$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Insertion one operation
nodes.statement: It seems natural to define $I_1(R)$ as $\iota^2``V \times R$; this requires no new axiom.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Insertion one on n-ary relations
nodes.statement: Define $I_{1,n}(R)$ as $\iota^{2(n-1)}``V \times R$: this is correct for prepending all possible initial projections to an $n$-tuple.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Iterated insertion one
nodes.statement: Then define $I^1_{1,n}(R)$ as $I_{1,n}(R)$ and define $I^{m+1}_{1,n}(R)$ as $I_{1,n+m}(I^m_{1,n}(R))$: this takes into account the fact that the tuples get longer. The intention here is that $I^m_{1,n}$ represents the result of applying the insertion one operation to an $n$-ary relation $m$ times, yielding an $(n+m)$-ary relation.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Insertion two on n-ary relations
nodes.statement: Define $I_{2,n}(R)$ and $I^1_{2,n}(R)$ as $I_2(R) \cap V^{n+1}$ [one effect of the intersection with $V^{n+1}$ is to restrict second projections of tuples in $I_2(R)$ to appropriately iterated singletons], and define $I^{m+1}_{2,n}(R)$ as $I_{2 ,n+m}(I^m_{2,n}(R))$: this takes into account the fact that the tuples get longer. The intention here is that $I^m_{2,n}$ represents the result of applying the insertion two operation to an $n$-ary relation $m$ times, yielding an $(n+m)$-ary relation.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: type lowering axiom
nodes.statement: $(\forall x:(\exists y:(\forall z:z \in y \leftrightarrow (\forall w:(w,\{z\}) \in x))))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Type lowering operation
nodes.statement: We define ${\tt TL}(x)$ by $(\forall z:z \in {\tt TL}(x) \leftrightarrow (\forall w:(w,\{z\}) \in x))$. This is a very strange operation!
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Inverse singleton image
nodes.statement: We define $\iota^{-1}``x$ as ${\tt TL}(V \times x)$. This is the set of all elements of singletons belonging to $x$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Elementwise singleton image
nodes.statement: We can then define $\iota``x$, the elementwise image of $x$ under the singleton operation, as $\iota^{-1}``(\iota^2``(x))$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Iterated singleton images
nodes.statement: Further, we define $\iota^{-(n+1)}``(x)$ as $\iota^{-1}``(\iota^{-n}``(x))$ for each concrete natural number $n$, and $\iota^{n+1}``(x)$ as $\iota``(\iota^{n}``(x))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Range and domain of a relation
nodes.statement: We develop an important operation step by step. ${\tt TL}(R) = \{z:(\forall w:(w,\{z\})\in R)\}$ Dually, $({\tt TL}(R^c))^c = \{z:(\exists w:(w,\{z\})\in R)\}$ Now $({\tt TL}((R^\iota)^c))^c = \{z:(\exists w:(w,\{z\})\in R^\iota)\}$, which is the same as $({\tt TL}((R^\iota)^c))^c = \{z:(\exists w:(\{w\},\{z\})\in R^\iota)\}$ because all elements of the domain of $R^{\iota}$ are singletons, which is the same as $({\tt TL}((R^\iota)^c))^c = \{z:(\exists w:(w,z)\in R)\}$ so we define ${\tt rng}(R)$ as $({\tt TL}((R^\iota)^c))^c$, and define ${\tt dom}(R)$ as ${\tt rng}(R^{-1})$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates
nodes.statement_short: Range of $R$ defined via type lowering of the complement of $R^\iota$; domain as range of the converse.

nodes.name: subset axiom
nodes.statement: $(\exists x:(\forall yz:(y,z) \in x \leftrightarrow (\forall w:w \in y \rightarrow w \in z)))$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Subset relation as a set
nodes.statement: We define $[\subseteq]$ as the intersection of a set provided by the previous axiom with $V \times V$: $[\subseteq]$ is the set of all ordered pairs $(x,y)$ such that $x \subseteq y$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Membership relation as a set
nodes.statement: We define $[\in]$ as $[\subseteq]\cap (1 \times V)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Verification that the Hailperin axioms give comprehension
nodes.statement: What we need to do is verify that $\{x:\phi\}$ exists for each formula $\phi$ of the language of TST, to ensure that comprehension holds. We do this by induction on the structure of formulas. $\{x:\neg \phi\}$ is $\{x :\phi\}^c$. $\{x :\phi \wedge \psi\}$ is $\{x:\phi \} \cap \{x:\psi\}$. Now we have the much more complex task of analyzing $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}.$$ Choose a type $\tau'$ higher than the type $\tau_i$ of each $t_i$. Do this for bound variables as well, and further, in each formula $(\forall t_i:\psi)$ or $(\exists t_i:\psi)$ we require that all occurrences of $t_i$ be free in $\psi$ and the index of $t_i$ be less than the index of any other variable appearing free in $\psi$. It should be clear that we can do this without loss of generality. Where the type of $t_i$ is $\tau_i$, we define $x_i$ as $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)$: we construct $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}$$ by defining manipulations which allow us to build sets $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):\phi^*(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\}$ in which all the variables are of the same type. We write $\phi^*$ to suggest that the formula $\phi$ must be transformed to effect our change of variables: $t_i = t_j$ is equivalent to $x_i = x_j$, and $t_i \in t_j$ is equivalent to $(x_i,x_j) \in [\in]^{\iota^{\tau'-\tau_j}}$ (the reader will see that we use this representation below, though embedded in larger tuples). A quantifier over $t_i$ is equivalent to a quantifier over $x_i$ restricted to $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}``V$. For any such representation, we have a type signature $$\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}``V \times \ldots \times \iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}``V.$$ We abbreviate this as $\tau^*$. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_1 = x_n\}$ is obtained as $I_{2,2}^{n-2}(\iota^2``V)\cap \tau^*$. The set $\{(x_1,\dots,x_n):x_1 = x_i\}$ ($i<n$) is obtained as $I_{2,3}^{i-2}(I_3(\iota^2``V))\cap \tau^*$. We then can represent the set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = x_j\}$ (wlog $i<j$) as \newline $I_{1,n-i+1}^{i-1}(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-i+1}):x_1 = x_{j-i+1}\})\cap \tau^*$. The set $\{(\{x_1\},x_2):x_1 \in x_2\}$ has already been defined above as $[\in]$. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists uv:x_i = \iota^{k+1}(u) \wedge x_j = \iota^k(v) \wedge u\in v)\}$ is $${\tt rng}^2(I_3(R^{\iota^{k+2n}}[\in]) \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_1 = x_{i+2}\} \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_2=x_{j+2}\}).$$ This handles all representations of membership statements between $x_i$'s in the framework we are using. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists x_1:(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in R)\}$ is representable as $I_{1,n-1}({\tt rng}(R))$. This only allows us to quantify over the lowest numbered variable. This is actually sufficient. We have renamed bound variables so that all bound variables with different binders are distinct and in any subformula $(\exists y:\psi)$ $y$ will have lower index than any variable free in $\psi$. Then the quantified variable might not be $x_1$, but if it is $x_k$, we can use the representation $I^{k}_{1,n-k}({\tt rng}^k(R))$: strip off the first $k-1$ variables, which are dummies already quantified over, quantify over $x_k$ (stripping off one more variable) and put $k$ dummies back, as it were. This gives sufficient machinery to handle representations of all sentences in the language of TST (or stratified sentences in the language of NF) in the format we are using. However, the final representation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ obtained in this way will be of the form $R=\{(\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}(t_1),\ldots,\iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}(t_n)):\phi(t_1.\ldots,t_n)\}$ where some of the $t_i$'s are bound variables (all values of which will appear), and some are parameters. Let $P$ be the set of $i$ such that $t_i$ is a parameter. The final computation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ will be as $$\iota^{-(\tau'-\tau_{n})}``\left({\tt rng}^{n-1}\left(R \cap \bigcap_{i \in P}\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = \iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)\}\right)\right)$$ where a final bit of computation must be exhibited: $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = t\}$ is realized as $I^{i-1}_{1,2}(\{\iota^{2(n-i-1)}(t)\}\times V)\cap \tau^*.$
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates
nodes.statement_short: Induction on formulas: complements and intersections for connectives; quantifiers via tuples of iterated singletons manipulated by insertion and range operations.

nodes.name: Assessment of the Hailperin axiomatization
nodes.statement: We state for the record that we think this is a bad finite axiomatization of NF, or finite template axiomatization of TST: we think the treatment of $n$-tuples is terribly difficult to work with. But it does work, and the second author chose to verify the consistency of TTT by verifying that the finite (template) axiomatization is satisfied in the structure for the language of TTT that we define, so it merits discussion here. It should be noted that any finite template axiomatization of TST could be used; there is no advantage to this one for the formalization, and there is an oddity, because the one impredicative axiom (the axiom of type lowering) does a lot of extra work, since it is also essential for constructing domains and ranges of functions. In the formalization, the proof of type lowering was in effect divided into the proof of the existence of $\iota^3``{\tt TL}(x)$, which is predicative, and the proof of the existence of set unions of sets of singletons.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Type index order
nodes.statement: Types are indexed by a well-ordering $\leq_\tau$ (from which we define a strict well-ordering $<_\tau$ in the obvious way).
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Type indices
nodes.statement: We refer to elements of the domain of $\leq_\tau$ as ``type indices".
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Supertype
nodes.statement: For each element $t$ of ${\tt dom}(\leq_\tau)$ we will define a set $\tau^*_t$, called supertype $t$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Base supertype
nodes.statement: If $m$ is the minimal element of the domain of $\leq_\tau$, we choose a set $\tau^*_m$ as supertype $m$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Construction of higher supertypes
nodes.statement: We describe the construction of $\tau^*_t$, assuming that $t \in {\tt dom}(\leq_\tau)$ and $t \neq m$ and for all $u <_\tau t$, we have defined $\tau^*_u$. We define $\tau^*_t$ as $$\left\{X \cup \{\{\tau^*_u:u <_\tau t\}\}:X \subseteq \bigcup_{u <_\tau t}\tau^*_u\right\}.$$
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework
nodes.statement_short: Supertype $t$ consists of all subsets of the union of lower supertypes, each tagged with the label $\{\tau^*_u:u<_\tau t\}$.

nodes.name: Labelling element of a supertype
nodes.statement: An element of supertype $t>_\tau m$ is a subset of the union of all lower types, with $t^+ = \{\tau^*_u:u <_\tau t\}$ added as an element.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Foundation keeps supertypes disjoint
nodes.statement: Foundation in the metatheory ensures a clean construction here. An element $x$ of supertype $t>_\tau m$ is always nonempty with $t^+$ as an element. The set $t^+$ has supertype $u$ as an element for each $u <_\tau t$, so $t^+$ and so $x$ cannot belong to any supertype $u$ with $u <_\tau t$, by foundation. The labelling element $t^+$ cannot belong to supertype $t$ by foundation, because an element of supertype $t$ must be nonempty and have $t^+$ as an element. Further, $t^+$ cannot belong to any supertype $v$ with $t <_\tau v$, because any element of $v$ contains $v^+$ as an element which contains supertype $t$ as an element and any element of supertype $t$ contains $t^+$ as an element, so $t^+ \in v$ would violate foundation in the metatheory.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Membership relations of the supertype structure
nodes.statement: The membership relations of this structure are transparent: $x \in_{t,u} y$ ($t <_\tau u$) is defined as $x \in \tau^*_t \wedge y \in \tau^*_u \wedge x \in y$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Supertypes are not a model of TTT
nodes.statement: The system of supertypes is certainly not a model of TTT, because it does not satisfy extensionality. It is easy to construct many sets in a higher type with the same extension over a given lower type, by modifying the other extensions of the object of higher type.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Supertypes satisfy TTT comprehension
nodes.statement: The system of supertypes does satisfy the comprehension scheme of TTT.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework
conclusions: The system of supertypes does satisfy the comprehension scheme of TTT

nodes.name: Crabbé's interpretation of NFU in stratified comprehension
nodes.statement: One can use Jensen's method to construct a model of stratified comprehension with no extensionality axiom from the system of supertypes, and stratified comprehension with no extensionality axiom interprets NFU in a manner described by Marcel Crabb\'e in \cite{marcelsf}.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework
conclusions: stratified comprehension with no extensionality axiom interprets NFU

nodes.name: Generality of the system of supertypes
nodes.statement: Any model of TTT (assuming there are any) is isomorphic to a substructure of a system of supertypes.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework
assumptions: Any model of TTT
conclusions: is isomorphic to a substructure of a system of supertypes

nodes.name: Proof of the generality of supertypes
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a model of TTT (more generally, any structure for the language of TTT in which each object outside the base type is determined given all of its extensions). Let $\leq_M$ be the well-ordering on the types of $M$ and let $m$ be the minimal type of $M$. We will assume as above that $\leq_\tau$ is a well-ordering of type labels $t$ with corresponding actual types $\tau_t$ of $M$: of course, we could use the actual types of $M$ as type indices, but we preserve generality this way. We also assume that the sets implementing the types of $M$ are disjoint (it is straightforward to transform a model in which the sets implementing the types are not disjoint to one in which they are, without disturbing its theory, by replacing each $x \in \tau_t$ with $(x,t)$). We consider the supertype structure generated by ${\leq_\tau}:={\leq_M}$ and $\tau^*_m := \tau_m$. We indicate how to define an embedding from $M$ into this supertype structure. Define $I(x) = x$ for $x \in \tau_m = \tau^*_m$. If we have defined $I$ on each type $u <_\tau t$, we define $I(x)$, for $x \in \tau_t$, as $$\bigcup_{u <_\tau t} \{I(y):y \in^M_{u,t} x\} \cup \{\{\tau^*_u:u <_\tau t\}\}.$$ It should be clear that as long as $M$ satisfies the condition that an element of any type other than the base type is uniquely determined given all of its extensions in lower types, $I$ is an isomorphism from $M$ to a substructure of the stated system of supertypes. A model of TTT, in which any one extension of an element of any higher type in a lower type exactly determines the object of higher type, certainly satisfies this condition. So the problem of constructing a model of TTT is equivalent to the problem of constructing a model of TTT which is a substructure of a supertype system.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework
nodes.statement_short: Embed a model $M$ into the supertype structure built on its type order by recursively mapping each element to the set of images of its members plus the label.

nodes.name: Extensions in supertypes vs types
nodes.statement: Notice that if $\alpha>_\tau \beta$ are supertypes, and $x \in \tau^*_\alpha$, $x \cap \tau^*_\beta$ is the extension of $x$ over supertype $\beta$. This will be inherited by a scheme of types $\tau_\gamma$ with each $\tau_\gamma \subseteq \tau^*_\gamma$ if an additional condition holds: for $\alpha>_\tau\beta$, we will have for $x \in \tau_\alpha$ that $x \cap \tau^*_\beta$ is the extension of $x$ over supertype $\beta$ as already noted: for it to be the extension over type $\beta$ we need the general condition $x \cap \tau^*_\delta \subseteq \tau_\delta$ for all $\gamma>\delta$ and $x \in \tau_\gamma$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Model parameters
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a limit ordinal. Let $\leq_\tau$ be the order on $\lambda \cup \{-1\}$ which has $-1$ as minimal and agrees otherwise with the usual order on $\lambda$. Let $\kappa$ be an uncountable regular cardinal (that is, an uncountable regular initial ordinal). Sets of cardinality $<\kappa$ we call {\em small\/}. Sets which are not small we may call {\em large\/}. We make no assumption about the relative sizes of $\kappa$ and $\lambda$. Let $\mu$ be a strong limit cardinal with $\kappa<\mu$, $\lambda \leq \mu$ and with the cofinality of $\mu$ at least ${\tt max}(\kappa,\lambda)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.statement_short: Fix a limit ordinal $\lambda$, an uncountable regular $\kappa$ (sets below $\kappa$ are small), and a strong limit $\mu>\kappa$ with cofinality at least $\max(\kappa,\lambda)$.
nodes.label: def:model_params

nodes.name: Minimal model parameters
nodes.statement: The minimal model parameters are $\lambda = \omega, \kappa = \omega_1, \mu = \beth_{\omega_1}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.label: rk:example_model_params

nodes.name: Base type of atoms
nodes.statement: Let $\tau^*_{-1}=\tau_{-1}$ be $$\{(\nu,\beta,\gamma,\alpha):\nu<\mu \wedge \beta \in \lambda\cup \{-1\} \wedge \gamma \in \lambda \setminus \{\beta\}\wedge \alpha<\kappa\}.$$ Note that this completes the definition of the supertype structure we are working in as defined in section \ref{ss:supertype_framework}: we now have a definite reference for $\tau^*_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in \lambda$. The important part of this definition is that $\tau_{-1}^*$ has size $\mu$; the precise form of $\tau_{-1}^*$ is chosen to aid with definition \ref{def:f_map}. This type, while important for the model construction, will not be part of our final model of TTT; the types of the final model will be indexed by $\lambda$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.statement_short:
Type $-1$ is the set of quadruples $(
u, eta,\gamma,\alpha)$ with $
u<\mu$, $\gamma
e eta$, $\alpha<\kappa$; it has size $\mu$.
nodes.label: def:supertypes

nodes.name: Type index membership notation
nodes.statement: Notice that if $\alpha,\beta$ are type indices, $\alpha\in \beta$ is a convenient short way to say $-1 <_\tau \alpha <_\tau \beta$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction

nodes.name: Extended type index
nodes.statement: A nonempty finite subset of $\lambda \cup \{-1\}$ {with minimum element $-1$} may be termed an {\em extended type index}. If $A$ is a finite subset of $\lambda\cup \{-1\}$ with at least two elements, $A_1$ is defined as $A \setminus \{{\tt min}(A)\}$, and further $A_{n+1}$ is defined as $(A_n)_1$ where this makes sense: the notation $A_2$ for $(A_1)_1$ sees use.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.label: def:extended_type_index

nodes.name: Atoms, litters and near-litters
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.statement_short: Atoms are elements of $\tau_{-1}$; litters are the $\kappa$-sized blocks $L_{\nu,\beta,\gamma}$; near-litters differ from a litter by a small set.
nodes.label: def:atom_litter_near_litter

nodes.name: Near-litters as extensions of amorphous sets
nodes.statement: In our model, any near-litter will be the extension of $\kappa$-amorphous sets in each type above the base type, and we will use these amorphous sets to limit how much the model knows about the relationship between the different extensions of a model element.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction

nodes.name: Count of near-litters
nodes.statement: There are exactly $\mu$ near-litters.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
conclusions: There are exactly $\mu$ near-litters.
nodes.label: def:count_near_litters

nodes.name: Proof of the count of near-litters
nodes.statement:
A near-litter is determined as the symmetric difference of a litter $L$ (there are $\mu$ litters) and a small subset of $	au_{-1}$. So it is sufficient to show that a set of size $\mu$ has no more than $\mu$ small subsets. As $\mu$ has cofinality at least $\kappa$, each small subset of $\mu$ has a strict upper bound $
u<\mu$, and so is an element of $ igcup_{
u < \mu} \mathcal P(
u)$. But as $\mu$ is a strong limit cardinal, each $\mathcal P(
u)$ has size less than $\mu$, so there are only $\mu$ bounded subsets of $\mu$; in particular, there are only $\mu$ small subsets of $\mu$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction
nodes.statement_short: A near-litter is a litter modulo a small set; cofinality and strong-limit properties of $\mu$ bound small subsets of $\mu$ by $\mu$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis I1: lower extensions lie in lower types
nodes.statement: We assume that for $\gamma<\beta<\alpha$, if $x \in \tau_\beta$, $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma \subseteq \tau_\gamma$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion

nodes.name: Hypothesis I2: each type has cardinality mu
nodes.statement: We suppose that each $\tau_\beta$ already constructed is of cardinality $\mu$. Note that we already know that $\tau_{-1}$ is of cardinality $\mu$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We suppose that each $\tau_\beta$ already constructed ($\beta<_\tau \alpha$) is of cardinality $\mu$. Note that we already know that $\tau_{-1}$ is of cardinality $\mu$ (\textbf{I\ref{ih:cardinality}}).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I3: supports are defined at lower types
nodes.statement: We further intimate that for each $x \in \tau_\gamma$, $-1\leq \gamma<\alpha$, we have defined objects $S$ for which we say that $S$ is a $\gamma$-support of $x$. [This is introduced before the definition of support is actually given in \ref{def:support}, but there is no technical obstacle to defining supports earlier if desired].
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We further intimate that for each $x \in \tau_\gamma$, $-1\leq \gamma<\alpha$, we have defined objects $S$ for which we say that $S$ is a support of $x$ (\textbf{I\ref{ih:supports}}).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I4: position functions on supported elements
nodes.statement: We define $\tau_\beta^+$ for any type index $\beta$ as the collection of $(x,S)$ where $x \in \tau_\beta$ and $S$ is a support of $x$. We assume that we are provided with a well-ordering $\leq^+_\gamma$ of order type $\mu$ of $\tau_\gamma^+$ ($-1 \leq \gamma <\alpha$), by postulating an injection $\iota^+_\gamma$ from $\tau_\gamma^+$ into $\mu$ (it does not need to be onto) and defining $x \leq^+_\gamma y$ as $\iota^+_\gamma(x) \leq \iota^+_\gamma(y)$. For any model element $x$ and support $S$ of $x$, we define $\iota^+_*(x,S)$ as $\iota^+_\gamma(x,S)$, where $x \in \tau_\gamma$. [Hypotheses of the recursion about maps $\iota^+_\gamma$ are stated {in (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position_constraints}})}].
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We also provide a well-ordering $\leq^+_\gamma$ of order type $\mu$ of $\tau_\gamma^+$ ($-1 \leq \gamma <\alpha$), by postulating an injection $\iota^+_\gamma$ from $\tau_\gamma^+$ into $\mu$ (it does not need to be onto) and defining $x \leq^+_\gamma y$ as $\iota^+_\gamma(x) \leq \iota^+_\gamma(y)$ (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position}}).
For the moment, we define $\tau_\gamma^+$ as the set of all $(x,S)$ for which $x \in \tau_\gamma$ and $S$ is a support of $x$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis I5: typed near-litters exist uniquely
nodes.statement: We provide that for every near litter $N$ and every $\beta<\alpha$, there is a unique element $N_\beta$ of $\tau_\beta$ such that $N_\beta \cap \tau_{-1}=N$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We provide that for every near litter $N$ and every $\beta<\alpha$, there is a unique element $N_\beta$ of $\tau_\beta$ such that $N_\beta \cap \tau_{-1}=N$ ((\textbf{I\ref{ih:typed_near_litter}}): we will quite shortly give a precise description of all extensions of this object).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I6: extensionality at lower types
nodes.statement: We further stipulate that extensionality holds for each $\beta\in \alpha$: that is, for each $\gamma\in \beta$, any $x \in \tau_\beta$ is uniquely determined by $x \cap \tau_\gamma$; $x$ is uniquely determined by $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ only on the additional assumption that $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ is nonempty.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We further stipulate (\textbf{I\ref{ih:extensionality}}) that extensionality holds for each $\beta\in \alpha$: that is, for each $\gamma\in \beta$, any $x \in \tau_\beta$ is uniquely determined by $x \cap \tau_\gamma$; $x$ is uniquely determined by $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ only on the additional assumption that $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ is nonempty.

nodes.name: Hypothesis I7: position of typed near-litters
nodes.statement: We assert that $\iota_*(N) \leq \iota_*^+(N_\delta,S)$ will hold for any near litter $N$ and support $S$ of $N_\delta$, $\delta<\alpha$. This depends on the definition of the position function $\iota_*$ which appears below at a convenient point but involves no recursion. (\textbf{I\ref{ih:pos_typed_near_litter}}) appears in (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position_constraints}}), but is mentioned earlier here because it is used earlier in the argument.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: An additional property involving $\iota_*$ which is enforced by inductive hypotheses explained later about the maps $\iota_\beta^+$ is that $\iota_*(N) \leq \iota_*^+(N_\delta,S)$ will hold for any near litter $N$ and support $S$ of $N_\delta$ (\textbf{I\ref{ih:pos_typed_near_litter}}).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I8: elements are pre-extensional
nodes.statement: We presume that all elements of $\tau_\beta$, $\beta\in \alpha$, are pre-extensional {(definition \ref{def:pre_extensional})}.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We presume that all elements of $\tau_\beta$, $\beta\in \alpha$, are pre-extensional (\textbf{I\ref{ih:pre_extensional}}).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I9: elements are extensional
nodes.statement: We assume that all elements of $\tau_\beta$'s already constructed are extensional {(definition \ref{def:extensional})}.
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion
also_stated_at: We assume that all elements of $\tau_\beta$'s already constructed are extensional (\textbf{I\ref{ih:extensional}}).

nodes.name: Hypothesis I10: elements have supports
nodes.statement: We stipulate that all elements of $\tau_\beta$ ($\beta\in\alpha$) have $\beta$-supports. {Supports are defined in definition \ref{def:support}.}
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion

nodes.name: Hypothesis I11: constraints on position functions
nodes.statement: The conditions constraining the choice of functions $\iota^+_\beta$ ($-1 \leq \beta < \alpha$) are \begin{enumerate} \item $\iota_*(t) < \iota^+_*(x,S)$ if $(t,A)$ is in the range of $S$ {(supports are functions; see definition \ref{def:support})} and $x$ is not a typed near-litter. \item $\iota_*(N) \leq \iota^+_*(N_\gamma,S)$ for each near-litter $N$ and support $S$ of $N_\gamma $ (which appeared earlier as (\textbf{I\ref{ih:pos_typed_near_litter}}) for reasons stated there; the notation $N_\gamma$ is defined in definition \ref{def:typed_objects}). \end{enumerate} We then define $x \leq^+_\beta y$ as $\iota^+_\beta(x) \leq \iota^+_\beta(y)$. {We will use the position functions $\iota^+_*$ to perform induction along each $\tau_\beta^+$; these constraints on $\iota^+_*$ ensure that objects that a model element depends on (in some suitable sense) are processed before it in the induction.}
nodes.section: 3.3 Hypotheses for the recursion

nodes.name: Cardinality of tau-plus
nodes.statement: It is a hypothesis of the recursion that $\tau_\gamma$ is of cardinality $\mu$, from which it follows that $\tau^+_\gamma$ is of cardinality $\mu$, since there are $\mu$ supports (as we will see when supports are defined).
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
conclusions: $\tau^+_\gamma$ is of cardinality $\mu$

nodes.name: Typed objects
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a subset of $\tau_\gamma$ and $\gamma<\beta$, we define $X_\beta$ as the unique element $Y$ of $\tau_\beta$ such that $Y \cap \tau_\gamma = X$ (if this exists). Of course, this notation is only usable to the extent that we suppose that extensionality holds. Notice that the notation $N_\beta$ is a case of this. If $N$ is a near-litter we refer to $N_\beta$ as a {\em typed near-litter\/} (of type $\beta$).
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.label: def:typed_objects

nodes.name: Position function for near-litters and singletons of atoms
nodes.statement: We posit a bijection $\iota_*$ from the set of all near-litters and singletons of atoms to $\mu$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $\iota_*(L) < \iota_*(\{a\})$ if $a \in L$ and $L$ is a litter. \item $\iota_*(N^\circ)<\iota_*(N)$ if $N$ is a near-litter which is not a litter \item $\iota_*(\{a\}) < \iota_*(N)$ if $a \in N \Delta N^\circ$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: A bijection $\iota_*$ from near-litters and atom singletons to $\mu$, placing litters before their atoms and near-litters after their litter and symmetric difference.
nodes.label: def:pos_atom_near_litter

nodes.name: Direct construction of the position function
nodes.statement: The function may be constructed directly: first choose an ordering of type $\mu$ on litters, then put singletons of atoms directly after the litter they are inside (and before all later litters), then put near-litters after the corresponding litter and all singletons of atoms in the symmetric difference, then map each near-litter or singleton of an atom to its position in the resulting order.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: Order litters in type $\mu$, insert atom singletons after their litter and near-litters after their litter and atoms; take positions.

nodes.name: Room argument for the position function
nodes.statement: We do not run out of room before finishing the construction because $\mu$ has cofinality at least $\kappa$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: Cofinality of $\mu$ at least $\kappa$ leaves room at every stage.

nodes.name: Position function generator
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a set of size at most $\mu$ and $f : X \to \mathcal P(\mu)$ is such that each $f(x)$ is bounded, then there is an injection $\iota : X \to \mu$ such that $\iota(x) \not\in f(x)$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
assumptions: $X$ is a set of size at most $\mu$
$f : X \to \mathcal P(\mu)$ is such that each $f(x)$ is bounded
conclusions: there is an injection $\iota : X \to \mu$ such that $\iota(x) \not\in f(x)$
nodes.label: lem:position_generator

nodes.name: Proof of the position function generator
nodes.statement: Choose a well-ordering $<_X$ of $X$ of type at most $\mu$. At each stage $x$, assume we have already constructed $\iota(y)$ for $y <_X x$. We then define $$ \iota(x) = \min \left(\mu \setminus f(x) \setminus \{ \iota(y) : y < x \}\right). $$ Note that as $f(x)$ is bounded in $\mu$, and $\mu$ has initial order type, the set $\mu \setminus f(x)$ is of cardinality $\mu$. Since $\{ \iota(y) : y < x \}$ has cardinality less than $\mu$, the difference must be nonempty, so the definition given always succeeds.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: Transfinite recursion along a well-ordering of $X$, choosing the least ordinal outside $f(x)$ and the earlier values.

nodes.name: Construction of the position function
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: Apply the position function generator twice (atom singletons, then near-litters) and order the results lexicographically on $3\times\mu$.

nodes.name: f maps
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: $f_{\beta,\gamma}$ injects $\tau_\beta^+$ into litters $L_{\nu,\beta,\gamma}$, choosing by recursion the least-positioned unused litter above the position of its argument.
nodes.label: def:f_map

nodes.name: Ranges of distinct f maps are disjoint
nodes.statement: Note that the ranges of distinct $f$ maps are disjoint sets.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
conclusions: the ranges of distinct $f$ maps are disjoint sets

nodes.name: Pre-extensional elements and distinguished extensions
nodes.statement: We define the notion of {\em pre-extensional\/} element of $\tau^*_\beta$ ($-1 <\beta \leq \alpha$). An element $x$ of $\tau^*_\beta$ is pre-extensional iff there is a $\gamma<\beta$ such that (1) $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma \subseteq \tau_\gamma$, and (2) $\gamma=-1$ if $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ is nonempty or if any $x \cap \tau_\delta$ ($\delta \in \beta$) is empty, and (3) for each $\delta \in \beta \setminus \{\gamma\}$, $$x \cap \tau_\delta= \{N_\delta:(\exists a \in x\cap \tau_\gamma:\exists S:N \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(a,S))\}.$$ We say for any $x \in \tau^*_\beta$ and $\gamma$ with this property that $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ is a {\em distinguished extension\/} of $x$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: $x$ is pre-extensional if one extension $x\cap\tau_\gamma$ (forced to be $-1$ in degenerate cases) determines all others through the $f$ maps.
nodes.label: def:pre_extensional

nodes.name: Extensions of typed near-litters are computable
nodes.statement: Note that we now know how to compute all other extensions of typed near-litters $N_\beta$, because the $-1$-extension of $N_\beta$ is distinguished and this indicates how to compute all the other extensions.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Alternate extension map
nodes.statement: For any $\delta \in \alpha$ and nonempty subset $a$ of type $\gamma \neq \delta$, we define $A_\delta(a)$ as $$\{N_\delta:(\exists x \in a:\exists S:N \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,S))\}.$$ For any nonempty subset $x$ of type $\delta$ there is at most one subset $y$ of any type such that $A_\delta(y)=x$. There cannot be more than one such $y$ in any given type because the $f$ maps are injective. There cannot be more than one such $y$ in different types because the ranges of $f$ maps with distinct index pairs are disjoint. We use the notation $A^{-1}(x)$ for this set if it exists, defining a very partial function $A^{-1}$ on nonempty subsets of types.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.label: def:a_map

nodes.name: Distinguished extension is the A-inverse image of the others
nodes.statement: Note that any distinguished extension of any type element $x$ is the image under $A^{-1}$ of its other extensions.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
conclusions: any distinguished extension of any type element $x$ is the image under $A^{-1}$ of its other extensions

nodes.name: Well-foundedness of A-inverse
nodes.statement: No nonempty subset of a type has infinitely many iterated images under $A^{-1}$, and there are no cycles in $A^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
conclusions: No nonempty subset of a type has infinitely many iterated images under $A^{-1}$
there are no cycles in $A^{-1}$
nodes.label: prop:a_map_well_founded

nodes.name: Proof of well-foundedness of A-inverse
nodes.statement: Let $a$ be a nonempty subset of type $\gamma$ for which $A^{-1}(a)$ exists. Since $A^{-1}(a)$ exists, every element of $a$ is of the form $N_\gamma$ where $N$ is a near-litter. Choose $N_\gamma \in a$ such that $\iota_*(N)$ is minimal. Note that $N$ is in fact a litter by the constraints in definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter}. Let $b = A^{-1}(a)$: we have $a = A_\gamma(b)$, where $b$ is a subset of some $\tau_\delta$ with $\delta \neq \gamma$. In particular, $N = f_{\delta,\gamma}(u,U)$ for some $u \in \tau_\delta$ and $U$ a support of $u$. If $u=M_\delta$ we can further state that $\iota_*(N) > \iota^+_*(M_\delta,U) \geq \iota_*(M)$: if $b$ itself has an image under $A^{-1}$, the minimum value of ordinals $\iota_*(M)$ for $M_\delta \in b$ will be less than the minimum value of ordinals $\iota_*(N)$ for $N_\gamma\in a$, which establishes that there is an ordinal parameter determined by a nonempty subset of a type which decreases strictly when $A^{-1}$ is applied (if it is applicable), and so no nonempty subset of a type can have infinitely many iterated images under $A^{-1}$, nor can there be any cycles in $A^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model
nodes.statement_short: The minimal position of the near-litters in a set strictly decreases under $A^{-1}$, so there are no infinite chains or cycles.
