nodes.section: 5.1 Ways in which this resolution of the NF consistency problem is unexciting

nodes.name: Global choice-like statements in NF
nodes.statement: Questions of consistency with NF of global choice-like statements such as ``the universe is linearly ordered" or the prime ideal theorem cannot be resolved by the method used here (at least, not without major changes).
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: No global linear order in these models
nodes.statement: Our models falsify the existence of a global linear order at the outset: a litter cannot be linearly ordered.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Internal well-orderings are well-orderings
nodes.statement: Note that in our models of TTT, any relation which the internal theory thinks is a well-ordering actually is a well-ordering.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements
conclusions: in our models of TTT, any relation which the internal theory thinks is a well-ordering actually is a well-ordering

nodes.name: Proof that internal well-orderings are well-orderings
nodes.statement: The reason is that in the metatheory any linear order which is not a well-ordering admits a countable set with no minimal element (the range of a strictly decreasing sequence). This requires choice, but choice holds in the metatheory. So, if a relation represented in the model of TTT is not a well-ordering from the standpoint of the metatheory, there is a countable subcollection of its domain which has no minimal element, and this countable subset is actually realized in the model of TTT, because our models of TTT are countably complete, so the model of TTT sees that the relation is not a well-ordering.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements
nodes.statement_short: A non-well-ordering has a countable descending witness in the metatheory, which the countably complete model contains.

nodes.name: Internal well-founded relations are well-founded
nodes.statement: Essentially the same argument shows that any relation which a model of TTT constructed by our method thinks is well-founded is actually well-founded in the sense of the metatheory.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Power sets of well-orderable sets are well-orderable
nodes.statement: In our models of TTT, the power set of any well-orderable set can be well-ordered.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements
assumptions: In our models of TTT
conclusions: the power set of any well-orderable set can be well-ordered

nodes.name: Proof that power sets of well-orderable sets are well-orderable
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a set in a model of TTT constructed by our method which admits a well-ordering (defined along a particular type sequence). The well-ordering $\leq_X$ of $X$ which we are given must have a support. A permutation which fixes the support of $\leq_X$ [in the appropriate sense defined in the paper] will fix $\leq_X$ and, because $\leq_X$ is a well-ordering in the sense of the metatheory, its action on the type of the elements of $X$ (in the type sequence with respect to which $\leq_X$ is a well-ordering) must fix each element of $X$, so in fact we have a common support for all elements of $X$, which in turn gives a support for each subcollection of $X$ in the sense of the metatheory as implemented in the appropriate type in the particular type sequence, so all of these are sets in the model of TTT (in the appropriate type in the particular type sequence) and further gives a support for the well-ordering of the power set of $X$ induced by any well-ordering of the power set of $X$ in the sense of the metatheory, so the power set of $X$ is well-ordered in the model of TTT.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements
nodes.statement_short: A support of the well-ordering fixes every element of $X$, giving a common support for all subsets and for any metatheoretic well-ordering of the power set.

nodes.name: Equivalent form: power set of the ordinals is well-orderable
nodes.statement: It is an interesting incidental remark that the theorem is equivalent in NF to the assertion that a single big power set, the power set of the set of ordinals, can be well-ordered, and this is seen to hold in models of NF constructed from our models of TTT.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Beth numbers are alephs in these models
nodes.statement: Applying the same technique to sets with well-founded extensional relations on them can be used to show that all $\beth$ numbers are alephs, and that the internal representation of an initial segment of the cumulative hierarchy using equivalence classes of well-founded extensional relations with top which is possible in TTT will agree precisely with the cumulative hierarchy in the metatheory as far as it goes (the internal representation will always give a proper initial segment of the hierarchy in the metatheory, of course).
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Strong unstratified axioms from strong partition properties
nodes.statement: NF with strong axioms such as the Axiom of Counting (introduced by Rosser in \cite{rosser}, an admirable textbook based on NF), the Axiom of Cantorian Sets (introduced in \cite{henson})\footnote{Getting Cantorian Sets or Large Ordinals to hold is sensitive to the relationship between $\kappa$ and $\lambda$. It requires the hypothesis that $\kappa<\lambda=\mu$ to avoid outright refutability of this axiom in resulting models of NF, and then a large cardinal hypothesis. We note that for the moment we need to use Henson's original formulation of the Axiom of Cantorian Sets, that any {\em well-orderable\/} cantorian set is strongly cantorian; the situation for non-well-orderable sets is not yet clear to us.} or my\footnote{The first author is speaking.} axioms of Small Ordinals and Large Ordinals (introduced in my \cite{mybook}, which pretends to be a set theory textbook based on NFU) can be obtained by choosing $\lambda$ large enough to have strong partition properties, more or less exactly as I report in my paper \cite{strongaxioms} on strong axioms of infinity in NFU: the results in that paper are not all mine, and I owe a good deal to Robert Solovay in that connection (unpublished conversations and \cite{nfub}).
nodes.section: 5.3 Strong unstratified axioms for NF derived from strong partition properties

nodes.name: NF has alpha-models for each standard ordinal
nodes.statement: That NF has $\alpha$-models for each standard ordinal $\alpha$ follows by the same methods Jensen used for NFU in his original paper \cite{nfu}: the proof we give in subsection \ref{subsection:alpha_models} for the existence of $\alpha$-models is essentially the same as Jensen's, and a model of TTT constructed by our method will implement each ordinal $\alpha$ of the metatheory which is less than $\kappa$ (and we can choose $\kappa$ larger than any fixed $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ with cofinality greater than $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$).
nodes.section: 5.3 Strong unstratified axioms for NF derived from strong partition properties

nodes.name: No model of NF contains all countable subsets of its domain
nodes.statement: No model of NF can contain all countable subsets of its domain; all well-typed combinatorial consequences of closure of a model of TST under taking subsets of size $<\kappa$ will hold in our models, but the application of compactness which gets us from TST + Ambiguity to NF forces the existence of externally countable proper classes, a result which has long been known and which also holds in NFU.
nodes.section: 5.3 Strong unstratified axioms for NF derived from strong partition properties

nodes.name: omega-models of the theory of negative types
nodes.statement: The Theory of Negative Types of Hao Wang (TST with all integers as types, proposed in \cite{tnt}) has $\omega$-models; an $\omega$-model of NF gives an $\omega$-model of the theory of negative types immediately.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Existence of omega-models of the theory of negative types
nodes.statement: The question of existence of $\omega$-models of the theory of negative types was open.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Specker tree
nodes.statement: In ordinary set theory, the Specker tree of a cardinal is the tree in which the top is the given cardinal, the children of the top node are the preimages of the top under the map $(\kappa \mapsto 2^{\kappa})$, and the part of the tree below each child is the Specker tree of the child.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Forster's well-foundedness of Specker trees
nodes.statement: Forster proved using a result of Sierpi\'nski that the Specker tree of a cardinal must be well-founded (a result which applies in ordinary set theory or in NF(U), with some finesse in the definition of the exponential map in NF(U)).
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered
conclusions: the Specker tree of a cardinal must be well-founded

nodes.name: Consistency of a Specker tree of infinite rank
nodes.statement: The question which was open was whether existence of a Specker tree of infinite rank is consistent.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Specker tree of the universe under Counting
nodes.statement: It is known that in NF with the Axiom of Counting the Specker tree of the cardinality of the universe is of infinite rank.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Construction of models with a Specker tree of infinite rank
nodes.statement: Our methods show the existence of a model of NF with the Axiom of Counting. This gives us a model of TST in which the Specker tree of some cardinal is of infinite rank. It is straightforward to produce a model of bounded Zermelo set theory either with atoms or with extensionality and failure of foundation from a model of TST, which will satisfy the same stratified sentences: identify the elements of type 0 either as atoms or with their own singletons, then implement elements of each type $i+1$ as subsets of type $i$ as guided by the original model of TST, identifying type $i+1$ objects with elements of lower types which have been assigned the same extension.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered
nodes.statement_short: An NF + Counting model gives a TST model with an infinite-rank Specker tree, converted to a bounded Zermelo model with atoms or without foundation.

nodes.name: Bounded Zermelo model with a Specker tree of infinite rank
nodes.statement: This shows that we can get a model of bounded Zermelo set theory with atoms or without foundation in which there is a cardinal with Specker tree of infinite rank.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered
conclusions: we can get a model of bounded Zermelo set theory with atoms or without foundation in which there is a cardinal with Specker tree of infinite rank

nodes.name: ZFA model with a Specker tree of infinite rank
nodes.statement: It is straightforward with our methods to get a model of TTT with the Axiom of Counting with inaccessibles cofinal in $\lambda$, and in this model we will have an inaccessible greater than a cardinal with Specker tree of infinite rank, and so a model of ZFA in which there is a cardinal with Specker tree of infinite rank.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Specker tree of infinite rank in ZF
nodes.statement: The further question remains as to whether it is consistent with ZF that there is a cardinal with Specker tree of infinite rank.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: NF is no stronger than TST + Infinity
nodes.statement: We believe that NF is no stronger than TST + Infinity, which is of the same strength as Zermelo set theory with separation restricted to bounded formulas (\cite{kemeny}).
nodes.section: 5.5 The question of consistency strength
conclusions: NF is no stronger than TST + Infinity

nodes.name: What do models of NF look like in general?
nodes.statement: Another question of a very general and amorphous nature which remains is: what do models of NF (or TTT) look like in general? Are all models of NF in some way like the ones we describe, or are there models of quite a different character?
nodes.section: 5.6 The wide open question: what do models of NF look like in general?

nodes.name: From NF(U) to TTT(U)
nodes.statement: Suppose NF(U) is consistent. Let $(M,E)$ be a model of NF(U) (a set $M$ with a membership relation $E$). Implement type $\alpha$ as $M \times \{\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha<\lambda$. Define $E_{\alpha,\beta}$ for $\alpha<\beta$ as $\{((x,\alpha),(y,\beta)):xEy\}$. This gives a model of TTT(U). Empty sets in TTTU present no essential additional difficulties.
nodes.statement_short: Copy a model of NF(U) at every type to get a model of TTT(U).
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: From TTT(U) to NF(U)
nodes.statement: Suppose TTT(U) is consistent, and so we can assume we are working with a fixed model of TTT(U). Let $\Sigma$ be a finite set of sentences in the language of TST(U). Our first aim is to construct a model of TST(U) in which $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ holds for each sentence $\phi \in \Sigma$. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $n$ be the smallest natural number such that all variables which occur in $\Sigma$ have type less than $n$. We define a partition of the $n$-element subsets of $\lambda$. Each $A \in [\lambda]^n$ is put in a compartment determined by the truth values of the sentences $\phi^s$ in our model of TTT(U), where $\phi \in \Sigma$ and ${\tt rng}(s \restriction \{0,\ldots,n-1\}) = A$: there are no more than $2^{|\Sigma|}$ compartments. By Ramsey's theorem, there is an infinite set $H \subseteq \lambda$ homogeneous for this partition which includes the range of a strictly increasing sequence $h$. \item Any strictly increasing sequence $s$ determines a model of TST(U) in which each type $i$ is implemented as type $s(i)$ of our fixed model of TTT(U) and membership in the derived model of TST(U) of type $i$ objects in type $i+1$ objects is implemented as membership in the fixed model of TTT(U) of type $s(i)$ objects in type $s(i+1)$ objects. \item This model determined in this way by $h$ satisfies $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ for each $\phi \in \Sigma$. This achieves our first aim. \item But this implies by compactness that the full Ambiguity Scheme $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ is consistent with TST(U). We could at this point say that NF(U) is consistent by the 1962 result of Specker (\cite{ambiguity}), but we will continue and indicate how to prove this directly (our second aim). \item We pause to add a useful notion to our logic. The Hilbert symbol is a primitive term construction $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ (same type as $x$) with axiom schemes $(\exists x:\phi) \rightarrow \phi[(\epsilon x:\phi)/x]$ and $(\forall x:\phi \leftrightarrow \psi) \rightarrow (\epsilon x:\phi) = (\epsilon x:\psi)$ which cannot appear in instances of comprehension. We do not define the quantifiers in terms of the Hilbert symbol, because the quantifiers do need to appear in instances of comprehension. \item If we have a model of TST(U) augmented with a Hilbert symbol which satisfies Ambiguity (for all formulas, including those which mention the Hilbert symbol) then we can readily get a model of NF(U), by constructing a term model using the Hilbert symbol in the natural way, then identifying all terms with their type-raised versions (an element of the term model is a class of terms $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in the language of TST(U) which is obtained from a single such term by all possible upward or downward shifts of type by a constant amount: we write this $[(\epsilon x:\phi)]$). \item All statements in the resulting type-free theory can be decided: the truth value of a closed atomic formula $[(\epsilon x:\phi)] \,R\, [(\epsilon y:\psi)]$ in the model of NF(U) is determined by replacing each side of the formula with one of its elements in such a way as to get a well-typed formula, which will always be possible if types are taken high enough, and reading the truth value of the resulting formula from the model of TST(U) with Ambiguity and Hilbert symbol; $R$ is either = or $\in$ [note that the relation interpreting equality in the term model is a nontrivial equivalence relation]. Truth values of more complex statements are determined in standard ways. That this makes axioms of NF(U) true should be clear. \item Now observe that a model of TTT(U) can readily be equipped with a Hilbert symbol if this creates no obligation to add instances of comprehension containing the Hilbert symbol (use a well-ordering of the set implementing each type to interpret a Hilbert symbol $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in that type as the first $x$ such that $\phi$ or as a default object of the appropriate type if there is no such $x$), and the argument in paragraphs (1)--(4) adapts to show consistency of TST(U) plus Ambiguity with the Hilbert symbol. \item We remark that our method of proving (a version of) the Specker ambiguity result is distinctly different from the original method. Strictly speaking, we have only proved Specker's result for TST(U) + Ambiguity + existence of a Hilbert symbol, but that is all we need for our result. \item From this it follows that NF(U) is consistent under the hypothesis that TTT(U) is consistent, which is what was to be shown. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Derive NF(U) consistency from a model of TTT(U).
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Fix a model and a finite set of sentences
nodes.statement: Suppose TTT(U) is consistent, and so we can assume we are working with a fixed model of TTT(U). Let $\Sigma$ be a finite set of sentences in the language of TST(U). Our first aim is to construct a model of TST(U) in which $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ holds for each sentence $\phi \in \Sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a TTT(U) model and finite $\Sigma$; aim for TST(U) with ambiguity for $\Sigma$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 1: Ramsey homogeneous set
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be the smallest natural number such that all variables which occur in $\Sigma$ have type less than $n$. We define a partition of the $n$-element subsets of $\lambda$. Each $A \in [\lambda]^n$ is put in a compartment determined by the truth values of the sentences $\phi^s$ in our model of TTT(U), where $\phi \in \Sigma$ and ${\tt rng}(s \restriction \{0,\ldots,n-1\}) = A$: there are no more than $2^{|\Sigma|}$ compartments. By Ramsey's theorem, there is an infinite set $H \subseteq \lambda$ homogeneous for this partition which includes the range of a strictly increasing sequence $h$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $[\lambda]^n$ by truth values and take an infinite homogeneous set by Ramsey's theorem.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 2: TST(U) models from type sequences
nodes.statement: Any strictly increasing sequence $s$ determines a model of TST(U) in which each type $i$ is implemented as type $s(i)$ of our fixed model of TTT(U) and membership in the derived model of TST(U) of type $i$ objects in type $i+1$ objects is implemented as membership in the fixed model of TTT(U) of type $s(i)$ objects in type $s(i+1)$ objects.
nodes.statement_short: Each increasing type sequence yields a model of TST(U).
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 3: ambiguity for Sigma
nodes.statement: This model determined in this way by $h$ satisfies $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ for each $\phi \in \Sigma$. This achieves our first aim.
nodes.statement_short: The homogeneous sequence gives ambiguity for $\Sigma$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 4: compactness
nodes.statement: But this implies by compactness that the full Ambiguity Scheme $\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^+$ is consistent with TST(U). We could at this point say that NF(U) is consistent by the 1962 result of Specker (\cite{ambiguity}), but we will continue and indicate how to prove this directly (our second aim).
nodes.statement_short: Compactness gives consistency of TST(U) with the full Ambiguity Scheme.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 5: Hilbert symbol
nodes.statement: We pause to add a useful notion to our logic. The Hilbert symbol is a primitive term construction $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ (same type as $x$) with axiom schemes $(\exists x:\phi) \rightarrow \phi[(\epsilon x:\phi)/x]$ and $(\forall x:\phi \leftrightarrow \psi) \rightarrow (\epsilon x:\phi) = (\epsilon x:\psi)$ which cannot appear in instances of comprehension. We do not define the quantifiers in terms of the Hilbert symbol, because the quantifiers do need to appear in instances of comprehension.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Hilbert symbol, excluded from comprehension.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 6: term model
nodes.statement: If we have a model of TST(U) augmented with a Hilbert symbol which satisfies Ambiguity (for all formulas, including those which mention the Hilbert symbol) then we can readily get a model of NF(U), by constructing a term model using the Hilbert symbol in the natural way, then identifying all terms with their type-raised versions (an element of the term model is a class of terms $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in the language of TST(U) which is obtained from a single such term by all possible upward or downward shifts of type by a constant amount: we write this $[(\epsilon x:\phi)]$).
nodes.statement_short: Build a term model of Hilbert terms modulo type shifting.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 7: truth in the term model
nodes.statement: All statements in the resulting type-free theory can be decided: the truth value of a closed atomic formula $[(\epsilon x:\phi)] \,R\, [(\epsilon y:\psi)]$ in the model of NF(U) is determined by replacing each side of the formula with one of its elements in such a way as to get a well-typed formula, which will always be possible if types are taken high enough, and reading the truth value of the resulting formula from the model of TST(U) with Ambiguity and Hilbert symbol; $R$ is either = or $\in$ [note that the relation interpreting equality in the term model is a nontrivial equivalence relation]. Truth values of more complex statements are determined in standard ways. That this makes axioms of NF(U) true should be clear.
nodes.statement_short: Truth in the term model is read off from the ambiguous TST(U) model.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 8: Hilbert symbol in TTT(U)
nodes.statement: Now observe that a model of TTT(U) can readily be equipped with a Hilbert symbol if this creates no obligation to add instances of comprehension containing the Hilbert symbol (use a well-ordering of the set implementing each type to interpret a Hilbert symbol $(\epsilon x:\phi)$ in that type as the first $x$ such that $\phi$ or as a default object of the appropriate type if there is no such $x$), and the argument in paragraphs (1)--(4) adapts to show consistency of TST(U) plus Ambiguity with the Hilbert symbol.
nodes.statement_short: Well-orderings interpret a Hilbert symbol in TTT(U); the earlier argument adapts.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 9: comparison with Specker
nodes.statement: We remark that our method of proving (a version of) the Specker ambiguity result is distinctly different from the original method. Strictly speaking, we have only proved Specker's result for TST(U) + Ambiguity + existence of a Hilbert symbol, but that is all we need for our result.
nodes.statement_short: Remark that this proves the needed version of Specker's result.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Item 10: conclusion
nodes.statement: From this it follows that NF(U) is consistent under the hypothesis that TTT(U) is consistent, which is what was to be shown. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Conclude NF(U) consistency from TTT(U) consistency.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Reduction to a TTTU model
nodes.statement: It is enough to exhibit a model of TTTU.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to exhibiting a TTTU model.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Cumulative hierarchy model
nodes.statement: Represent type $\alpha$ as $V_{\omega+\alpha} \times \{\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha<\lambda$ ($V_{\omega+\alpha}$ being the rank indexed by $\omega+\alpha$ in the usual cumulative hierarchy). Define $\in_{\alpha,\beta}$ for $\alpha<\beta<\lambda$ as $$\{((x,\alpha),(y,\beta)):x \in V_{\omega+\alpha} \wedge y \in V_{\omega+\alpha+1} \wedge x \in y\}.$$ This gives a model of TTTU in which the membership of type $\alpha$ in type $\beta$ is defined in such a way that each $(y,\beta)$ with $y \in V_{\omega+\beta} \setminus V_{\omega+\alpha+1}$ is interpreted as an urelement over type $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Types are ranks $V_{\omega+\alpha}$; higher sets outside $V_{\omega+\alpha+1}$ act as urelements.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Infinity and Choice
nodes.statement: Our use of $V_{\omega+\alpha}$ enforces Infinity in the resulting models of NFU (note that we did not have to do this: if we set $\lambda=\omega$ and interpret type $\alpha$ using $V_\alpha$ we prove the consistency of NFU with the negation of Infinity). It should be clear that Choice (stated in a stratified way) holds in the models of NFU eventually obtained if it holds in the ambient set theory.
nodes.statement_short: Infinity and Choice transfer to the resulting NFU models.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Ordinariness of NFU
nodes.statement: This shows in fact that mathematics in NFU is quite ordinary (with respect to stratified sentences), because mathematics in the models of TSTU embedded in the indicated model of TTTU is quite ordinary. The notorious ways in which NF evades the paradoxes of Russell, Cantor and Burali-Forti can be examined in actual models and we can see that they work and how they work (since they work in NFU in the same way they work in NF).
nodes.statement_short: Mathematics in NFU is ordinary for stratified sentences.
nodes.section: 2.3 Tangled type theory TTT and TTTU

nodes.name: Relation to the earlier proof
nodes.statement: The proof is a modified version of the proof given above for consistency of NF(U), using a more powerful partition principle. We do not claim originality, referring the reader to \cite{nfu}, but our presentation is not the same, and it is adapted to talk of tangled type theory.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the NF(U) consistency proof with a stronger partition principle.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Recall the Erdős–Rado theorem
nodes.statement: The Erd\H{o}s--Rado theorem tells us that for a natural number $n\geq 1$ and an infinite cardinal $\mu$, any partition of $\exp^n(\mu)$ into $\mu$ compartments has a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$. This is not quite the usual formulation, but easily follows from it.
nodes.statement_short: State the Erdős–Rado partition theorem.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Ordinal constants and Hilbert symbol
nodes.statement: We extend the language of TTT(U) to include constant terms $\alpha^s$ and $\beta^s$ for each ordinal $\beta < \alpha$ of the metatheory for each sequence $s$ as described above. We similarly extend the language of TST(U) (in this case only needing constants $\alpha^i$ and $\beta^i$ for $\beta<\alpha$ for each $i\geq4$), and note that the translation of a sentence of TST(U) with language augmented with these ordinal constants into terms of a strictly increasing sequence of types in TTT(U) is straightforward, and we allow use of these constants in the comprehension axiom of TTT(U) as usual. We further include the Hilbert symbol in our language, with the same restriction stated above that the Hilbert symbol may not appear in instances of comprehension, noting our intention to construct a term model.
nodes.statement_short: Add ordinal constants and the Hilbert symbol to the languages.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Partitions by Hilbert-symbol values
nodes.statement: We consider partitions of $[\lambda]^n$ determined by the set $\Sigma_n$ of {\em all\/} closed Hilbert symbols (``closed" meaning the symbol contains no parameters) of the form $(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i < \alpha^i \wedge \phi)$ in the language of TST(U) augmented as indicated above and using only types less than $n$, with the compartment in the partition containing $A \in [\lambda]^n$ determined by the ordinal values $<\alpha$ [or default value, where we assume the default value is not an ordinal] assigned to all of these terms in our model of TTT(U) when types $0-(n-1)$ are replaced by the types in $A$ in increasing order in each of the Hilbert symbols in $\Sigma_n$. Here we are speaking loosely in that we say an ordinal $\gamma<\alpha$ is assigned as value to $(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i < \alpha^i \wedge \phi)$ when its value is in fact $\gamma^i$: it should be clear that this is unproblematic and easier to say.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $[\lambda]^n$ by the ordinal values of closed Hilbert symbols.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Counting compartments
nodes.statement: There are no more than $|\alpha|$ such Hilbert symbols, and no more than $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$ compartments in each of these partitions.
nodes.statement_short: At most $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$ compartments.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Hilbert values code truth values
nodes.statement: Note that assignment of values to all such Hilbert symbols induces a complete assignment of truth values to sentences of the extended language: $$(\epsilon \beta^i:\beta^i<\alpha \wedge \beta^i<2 \wedge (\beta=1 \leftrightarrow \phi))$$ codes a sentence $\phi$ into $\Sigma_n$ if $\phi$ mentions only types below $n > i$, because the assignment of ordinal value to this term corresponds to the assignment of truth value to $\phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Values of Hilbert symbols code truth values of sentences.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Homogeneous sets and cofinality
nodes.statement: The Erd\H{o}s--Rado theorem allows us to conclude that for any infinite $\mu<\lambda$, we have a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$ for the given partition in $\exp^n(\mu)<\lambda$. Further, we can find a single assignment of values to Hilbert symbols as described above which is associated with arbitrarily large homogeneous sets below $\lambda$, because the cofinality of $\lambda$ is greater than $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}$, the cardinality of the set of compartments in the partition, corresponding precisely to the cardinality of the set of such assignments of values. If we have chosen such an assignment of values for a specific value of $n$, we can further choose such an assignment of values for $n+1$ which extends it: for any $\mu$, choose a homogeneous set for the partition of $[\lambda]^n$ realizing the fixed assignment of values and of cardinality $\nu > \exp^{n+1}(\mu)$, then find a homogeneous set of size $\mu^+$ for the partition of $[\lambda]^{n+1}$ inside this homogeneous set, which will determine an assignment of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types extending the fixed one chosen for Hilbert symbols using $n$ types. Thus there are arbitrarily large homogeneous sets for assignments of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types extending the fixed one for Hilbert symbols using $n$ types. Thus there is a fixed assignment of values to Hilbert symbols using $n+1$ types which extends the given fixed assignment for $n$ types and which is associated with arbitrarily large homogeneous sets, by the already stated considerations of cofinality. Thus we can proceed through $\omega$ steps and find an assignment of values to all Hilbert symbols with the property that its restriction to any fixed number $n$ of types is realized in arbitrarily large homogenous sets below $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Erdős–Rado and cofinality give an assignment realized on arbitrarily large homogeneous sets, extended through all $n$.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Ambiguous complete theory
nodes.statement: Thus we have constructed a complete assignment of values to such Hilbert symbols in the extended TST(U) language, and thus a complete assignment of truth values to all sentences, which is ambiguous [invariant under displacement of types] and consistent with any statement holding at all sequences of types in the model of TTT(U). Thus for example we will get extensionality if the model of TTTU is actually a model of TTT. In fact, for any fixed $n$ all these assignments for Hilbert symbols mentioning only types less than $n$ will be realized at some sequence of types in the model of TTT(U) [verifying that this assignment of values is consistent and in effect a complete description of a model of NF(U)].
nodes.statement_short: The assignment is a complete ambiguous theory realized in the TTT(U) model.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Ordinal alpha is implemented
nodes.statement: Further, this model of NFU contains no ordinal less than what it calls $\alpha$ other than the ordinals which it calls $\beta$ for $\beta<\alpha$ in the metatheory, and the natural well-ordering on these ordinals is realized in the model of NF(U) and corresponds to a well-ordering of order type $\alpha$ in the metatheory. The reason for this is that the model of NFU is a term model, and any term denoting an ordinal less than $\alpha$ can be slightly modified to the exact form used in defining the partitions, and the process will assign that term a concrete value less than $\alpha$, an actual ordinal $\beta<\alpha$ of the metatheory, so the order on the ordinals $<\alpha$ in the model of NF(U) has order type $\alpha$ in the metatheory.
nodes.statement_short: In the term model the ordinals below $\alpha$ are exactly the standard ones.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 There are $\alpha$-models for every $\alpha$

nodes.name: Fix a model with disjoint types
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a model of TTT (more generally, any structure for the language of TTT in which each object outside the base type is determined given all of its extensions). Let $\leq_M$ be the well-ordering on the types of $M$ and let $m$ be the minimal type of $M$. We will assume as above that $\leq_\tau$ is a well-ordering of type labels $t$ with corresponding actual types $\tau_t$ of $M$: of course, we could use the actual types of $M$ as type indices, but we preserve generality this way. We also assume that the sets implementing the types of $M$ are disjoint (it is straightforward to transform a model in which the sets implementing the types are not disjoint to one in which they are, without disturbing its theory, by replacing each $x \in \tau_t$ with $(x,t)$).
nodes.statement_short: Fix $M$, its type order, and make its types disjoint.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Choose the supertype structure
nodes.statement: We consider the supertype structure generated by ${\leq_\tau}:={\leq_M}$ and $\tau^*_m := \tau_m$. We indicate how to define an embedding from $M$ into this supertype structure.
nodes.statement_short: Use the supertype structure on $M$'s type order with base type $\tau_m$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Recursive embedding
nodes.statement: Define $I(x) = x$ for $x \in \tau_m = \tau^*_m$. If we have defined $I$ on each type $u <_\tau t$, we define $I(x)$, for $x \in \tau_t$, as $$\bigcup_{u <_\tau t} \{I(y):y \in^M_{u,t} x\} \cup \{\{\tau^*_u:u <_\tau t\}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define the embedding $I$ by recursion on types.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: I is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: It should be clear that as long as $M$ satisfies the condition that an element of any type other than the base type is uniquely determined given all of its extensions in lower types, $I$ is an isomorphism from $M$ to a substructure of the stated system of supertypes. A model of TTT, in which any one extension of an element of any higher type in a lower type exactly determines the object of higher type, certainly satisfies this condition. So the problem of constructing a model of TTT is equivalent to the problem of constructing a model of TTT which is a substructure of a supertype system.
nodes.statement_short: Extensionality makes $I$ an isomorphism onto a substructure.
nodes.section: 3.1 The abstract supertype framework

nodes.name: Reduce to counting small subsets
nodes.statement: A near-litter is determined as the symmetric difference of a litter $L$ (there are $\mu$ litters) and a small subset of $\tau_{-1}$. So it is sufficient to show that a set of size $\mu$ has no more than $\mu$ small subsets.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to counting small subsets of a set of size $\mu$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction

nodes.name: Small subsets are bounded
nodes.statement:
As $\mu$ has cofinality at least $\kappa$, each small subset of $\mu$ has a strict upper bound $
u<\mu$, and so is an element of $ igcup_{
u < \mu} \mathcal P(
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Cofinality bounds each small subset.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction

nodes.name: Strong limit bound
nodes.statement: But as $\mu$ is a strong limit cardinal, each $\mathcal P(\nu)$ has size less than $\mu$, so there are only $\mu$ bounded subsets of $\mu$; in particular, there are only $\mu$ small subsets of $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong limit gives only $\mu$ bounded subsets.
nodes.section: 3.2 Preliminaries of the construction

nodes.name: Well-order X
nodes.statement: Choose a well-ordering $<_X$ of $X$ of type at most $\mu$. At each stage $x$, assume we have already constructed $\iota(y)$ for $y <_X x$.
nodes.statement_short: Well-order $X$ in type at most $\mu$ and recurse.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Recursive definition
nodes.statement: We then define $$ \iota(x) = \min \left(\mu \setminus f(x) \setminus \{ \iota(y) : y < x \}\right). $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose the least ordinal outside $f(x)$ and earlier values.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Room remains
nodes.statement: Note that as $f(x)$ is bounded in $\mu$, and $\mu$ has initial order type, the set $\mu \setminus f(x)$ is of cardinality $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu\setminus f(x)$ has size $\mu$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Recursion succeeds
nodes.statement: Since $\{ \iota(y) : y < x \}$ has cardinality less than $\mu$, the difference must be nonempty, so the definition given always succeeds.
nodes.statement_short: Fewer than $\mu$ values are used, so the choice always exists.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Positions of atom singletons
nodes.statement: First, let $\iota_0$ be any injection from the set of litters into $\mu$. Next, use lemma \ref{lem:position_generator}, with $X$ taken to be the collection of all singletons of atoms, setting $f(\{a\}) = \{ \nu : \nu \leq \iota_0(L) \}$ where $L$ is the unique litter such that $a \in L$, to create $\iota_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Inject litters, then place atom singletons above their litter.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Positions of near-litters
nodes.statement_short: Place near-litters above their litter and their symmetric-difference atoms.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Lexicographic merge
nodes.statement: Finally, we define a map $\iota$ from near-litters and singletons of atoms to $3 \times \mu$ by $$ g(x) = \begin{cases} (0, \iota_0(x)) & \text{if $x$ is a litter} \\ (1, \iota_1(x)) & \text{if $x$ is a singleton} \\ (2, \iota_2(x)) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ We can then define $\iota_*(x)$ to be the position of $g(x)$ in the restriction of the lexicographic order on $3 \times \mu$ to the image of $g$ (which is of order type $\mu$). The resulting function $\iota_*$ is then clearly a bijection, and has the required properties by construction, noting that near-litters that happen to be litters will automatically satisfy the third condition.
nodes.statement_short: Merge the three injections lexicographically into a bijection with $\mu$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Choose a minimal litter
nodes.statement: Let $a$ be a nonempty subset of type $\gamma$ for which $A^{-1}(a)$ exists. Since $A^{-1}(a)$ exists, every element of $a$ is of the form $N_\gamma$ where $N$ is a near-litter. Choose $N_\gamma \in a$ such that $\iota_*(N)$ is minimal. Note that $N$ is in fact a litter by the constraints in definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter}.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $a$ are typed near-litters; the one of minimal position is a litter.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Position decreases
nodes.statement: Let $b = A^{-1}(a)$: we have $a = A_\gamma(b)$, where $b$ is a subset of some $\tau_\delta$ with $\delta \neq \gamma$. In particular, $N = f_{\delta,\gamma}(u,U)$ for some $u \in \tau_\delta$ and $U$ a support of $u$. If $u=M_\delta$ we can further state that $\iota_*(N) > \iota^+_*(M_\delta,U) \geq \iota_*(M)$: if $b$ itself has an image under $A^{-1}$, the minimum value of ordinals $\iota_*(M)$ for $M_\delta \in b$ will be less than the minimum value of ordinals $\iota_*(N)$ for $N_\gamma\in a$, which establishes that there is an ordinal parameter determined by a nonempty subset of a type which decreases strictly when $A^{-1}$ is applied (if it is applicable), and so no nonempty subset of a type can have infinitely many iterated images under $A^{-1}$, nor can there be any cycles in $A^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The minimal position strictly decreases under $A^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Degenerate case
nodes.statement: If any $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ ($\gamma \in \beta$) is empty or if $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ is not empty, $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ is the unique distinguished extension (if it is empty of course it coincides with all the other extensions).
nodes.statement_short: If some extension is empty or the atom extension is nonempty, it is the unique distinguished one.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Main case
nodes.statement: So, what remains is the case of $x$ with $x \cap \tau_{-1}$ empty and each $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ nonempty for $\gamma<\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining case: atom extension empty, all others nonempty.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Assume two distinguished extensions
nodes.statement: Suppose that $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ and $x \cap \tau_\delta$ were both distinguished.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose two distinguished extensions.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: 2-cycle contradiction
nodes.statement: Then we would have $$ x \cap \tau_\gamma = A^{-1}(x \cap \tau_\delta) = A^{-1}(A^{-1}(x \cap \tau_\gamma)), $$ which contradicts proposition \ref{prop:a_map_well_founded} as this would imply that $A^{-1}$ has a cycle of length 2.
nodes.statement_short: This yields a 2-cycle of $A^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Common empty extension
nodes.statement: If two extensional model elements have an empty extension (over a type other than $\tau_{-1}$) in common, they both have all extensions empty and are equal.
nodes.statement_short: A common empty extension forces all extensions empty.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Common nonempty extension
nodes.statement: If two extensional model elements have a nonempty extension in common, it will be the distinguished extension of both, or a non-distinguished extension of both, since distinguished and non-distinguished extensions are taken from disjoint classes of subsets of types (when nonempty).
nodes.statement_short: A common nonempty extension is distinguished in both or neither.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Same distinguished extension
nodes.statement: In either case we deduce that the two elements have the same distinguished extension and thus have all extensions the same and are equal. Note that this gives weak extensionality over $\tau_{-1}$ (many objects have empty extension over type $-1$) but it gives full extensionality over any other type.
nodes.statement_short: Hence equal distinguished extensions and equal elements.
nodes.section: 3.4 Machinery for enforcing extensionality in the model

nodes.name: Recall the A map
nodes.statement: Recall that for nonempty $a\subseteq\tau_\gamma$ we defined $A_\delta(a)$ in definition \ref{def:a_map} as $$\{N_\delta:(\exists x \in a:(\exists S:N \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(a,S)))\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of $A_\delta$.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Commutation with A
nodes.statement: If $\pi$ is allowable of suitable index, $\pi_\delta``A_\delta(a)= A_\delta(\pi_\gamma``a)$ follows from the coherence condition. Verify this:
nodes.statement_short: Claim: allowable permutations commute with $A_\delta$ by coherence.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Forward inclusion
nodes.statement: Suppose we have $N_\delta$ with $x \in a$ such that $N \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,S)$. Then $$\pi_\delta(N_\delta) \cap \tau_{-1} = (\pi_\delta)_{-1}``N \sim (\pi_\delta)_{-1}``f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,S) \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(\pi_\gamma(x),\pi_\gamma[S]).$$ So any element of $\pi_\delta``A_\delta(a)$ is in $A_\delta(\pi_\gamma``a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Images of elements of $A_\delta(a)$ lie in $A_\delta(\pi_\gamma``a)$.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: Suppose we have $N_\delta$ with $x \in a$ such that $N \sim f_{\gamma,\delta}(\pi_\gamma(x),S)$. We then have $N \sim (\pi_\delta)_{-1}``f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,\pi_\gamma^{-1}[S])$. We want to show that $\pi_\delta^{-1}(N_\delta) \in A_\delta(a)$. We have $$\pi_\delta^{-1}(N_\delta) \cap \tau_{-1} = (\pi_\delta)_{-1}^{-1}``N \sim (\pi_\delta)_{-1}^{-1}``((\pi_\delta)_{-1}``f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,\pi_\gamma^{-1}[S])) = f_{\gamma,\delta}(x,\pi_\gamma^{-1}[S]),$$ establishing what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, preimages lie in $A_\delta(a)$.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Pre-extensionality preserved
nodes.statement: Notice that this shows that the coherence condition implies that the image under an allowable permutation of a pre-extensional element of our structure is pre-extensional.
nodes.statement_short: Hence pre-extensionality is preserved.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Parity of iterated images preserved
nodes.statement: Now this implies that if $a \subseteq \tau_\gamma$, then $A^{-1}(a)$ exists and is in $\tau_\delta$ exactly if $A^{-1}(\pi_\gamma``a)$ exists and is in $\tau_\delta$, and moreover $A^{-1}(\pi_\gamma``a)$ is equal to $\pi_\delta``A^{-1}(a)$ if it exists under these conditions. This verifies that the coherence condition implies that allowable permutations preserve full extensionality, not just pre-extensionality: the number of iterated images under $A^{-1}$ of an extension that exist is not affected by application of an allowable permutation in a suitable sense.
nodes.statement_short: Commutation with $A^{-1}$ preserves the parity of iterated images, so extensionality.
nodes.section: 3.5 Allowable permutations and supports

nodes.name: Empty case
nodes.statement: If $X$ is empty, then $X$ is simply the $\beta$-extension of the empty model element.
nodes.statement_short: Empty $X$ is the extension of the empty element.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Count iterated images
nodes.statement: Suppose $X$ is nonempty, and let $n$ be the number of iterated images that $X$ has under $A^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $n$ be the number of iterated $A^{-1}$-images of $X$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Even case
nodes.statement: If $n$ is even, consider the element $x \in \tau^*_\alpha$ such that $x \cap \tau^*_\beta = X$, $x \cap \tau^*_{-1} = \emptyset$, and whose other extensions at levels $-1 < \gamma < \alpha$, $\gamma \neq \beta$ are given by $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma = A_\gamma(X)$. We show this is a model element. Clearly each extension satisfies $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma \subseteq \tau_\gamma$. It is pre-extensional because $x \cap \tau_\beta$ is its distinguished extension, and it is extensional as $n$ is even. It has support $S$: if $\pi$ is $\alpha$-allowable and fixes $S$, then $\pi_\beta `` (x \cap \tau_\beta) = x \cap \tau_\beta$ by assumption, so by extensionality, $\pi$ must fix $x$. So $x \in \tau_\alpha$ and $x \cap \tau_\beta = X$.
nodes.statement_short: For even $n$, the element with distinguished extension $X$ is a model element.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Define the candidate element
nodes.statement: If $n$ is even, consider the element $x \in \tau^*_\alpha$ such that $x \cap \tau^*_\beta = X$, $x \cap \tau^*_{-1} = \emptyset$, and whose other extensions at levels $-1 < \gamma < \alpha$, $\gamma \neq \beta$ are given by $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma = A_\gamma(X)$. We show this is a model element. Clearly each extension satisfies $x \cap \tau^*_\gamma \subseteq \tau_\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $x$ with $\beta$-extension $X$ and other extensions $A_\gamma(X)$, then check it is a model element.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Pre-extensional and extensional
nodes.statement: It is pre-extensional because $x \cap \tau_\beta$ is its distinguished extension, and it is extensional as $n$ is even.
nodes.statement_short: Distinguished extension $X$ with even parity.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Support
nodes.statement: It has support $S$: if $\pi$ is $\alpha$-allowable and fixes $S$, then $\pi_\beta `` (x \cap \tau_\beta) = x \cap \tau_\beta$ by assumption, so by extensionality, $\pi$ must fix $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Permutations fixing $S$ fix $X$ and hence $x$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Conclusion of even case
nodes.statement: So $x \in \tau_\alpha$ and $x \cap \tau_\beta = X$.
nodes.statement_short: So $x$ is the required model element.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Odd case
nodes.statement: If $n$ is odd, let $Y = A^{-1}(X) \subseteq \tau_\gamma$. We claim that $S$ has the property that if $\pi$ is $\alpha$-allowable and $\pi[S] = S$, then $\pi_\gamma``Y = Y$. Indeed, as allowable permutations commute with $A$ maps by proposition \ref{prop:allowable_preserves_extensionality}, $$\pi_\gamma``Y = \pi_\gamma``A^{-1}(X) = A^{-1}(\pi_\beta``X) = A^{-1}(X) = Y.$$ This allows us to repeat the argument of the previous paragraph using $Y$ to obtain a model element $x \in \tau_\alpha$ satisfying $x \cap \tau_\gamma = Y$, where $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ is distinguished. Then, by pre-extensionality, we must have $x \cap \tau_\beta = A_\beta(x \cap \tau_\gamma) = X$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: For odd $n$, apply the even case to $Y=A^{-1}(X)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Let Y be the A-inverse
nodes.statement: If $n$ is odd, let $Y = A^{-1}(X) \subseteq \tau_\gamma$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: S also fixes Y
nodes.statement: We claim that $S$ has the property that if $\pi$ is $\alpha$-allowable and $\pi[S] = S$, then $\pi_\gamma``Y = Y$. Indeed, as allowable permutations commute with $A$ maps by proposition \ref{prop:allowable_preserves_extensionality}, $$\pi_\gamma``Y = \pi_\gamma``A^{-1}(X) = A^{-1}(\pi_\beta``X) = A^{-1}(X) = Y.$$
nodes.statement_short: Permutations fixing $S$ fix $Y$ since they commute with $A^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Apply even case to Y
nodes.statement: This allows us to repeat the argument of the previous paragraph using $Y$ to obtain a model element $x \in \tau_\alpha$ satisfying $x \cap \tau_\gamma = Y$, where $x \cap \tau_\gamma$ is distinguished.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain a model element with distinguished extension $Y$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Recover X
nodes.statement: Then, by pre-extensionality, we must have $x \cap \tau_\beta = A_\beta(x \cap \tau_\gamma) = X$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Pre-extensionality gives $x\cap\tau_\beta = X$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Merged support
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a support whose range is obtained from the unions of ranges of supports for each $x \in X$. Then, if $\pi[S] = S$, we have $$\pi_\beta``\left(\bigcup_{x \in X} x \cap \tau_\beta\right) = \bigcup_{x \in X} \pi_\beta``(x \cap \tau_\beta) = \bigcup_{x \in X} \pi(x) \cap \tau_\beta = \bigcup_{x \in X} x \cap \tau_\beta.$$
nodes.statement_short: Merge the supports of all members; it fixes the union.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Apply symmetric comprehension
nodes.statement: The conclusion then follows directly from symmetric comprehension.
nodes.statement_short: Apply symmetric comprehension.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Recall the generator
nodes.statement: We use the position function generator (proposition \ref{lem:position_generator}): recall that this states that if $X$ is a set of size at most $\mu$ and $f : X \to \mathcal P(\mu)$ is such that each $f(x)$ is bounded, then there is an injection $\iota : X \to \mu$ such that $\iota(x) \not\in f(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the position function generator.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Forbidden sets
nodes.statement: Setting $X = \tau^+_\beta$, we define $$ g(x, S) = \bigcup_{N \text{ s.t. } x = N_\delta} \iota_*(N) \cup \bigcup_{(y,A) \in {\tt rng}(S)} \iota_*(y) $$ and let $f(x, S) = \{ \nu : (\exists \xi \in g(x, S) : \nu \leq \xi) \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Forbid positions below those of related near-litters and support atoms.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Boundedness
nodes.statement: As $\mu$ has cofinality at least $\kappa$ and each $g(x, S)$ is small, each $f(x, S)$ is bounded as required.
nodes.statement_short: The forbidden sets are bounded, so the generator applies.
nodes.section: 3.6 Model elements defined

nodes.name: Freedom of action at delta
nodes.statement: The $\delta$-approximation $(\psi_{A_2})_\delta$ is coherent (remark \ref{rk:power_deriv_coherent}), so it approximates some $\delta$-allowable permutation $\pi$ by freedom of action.
nodes.statement_short: The derived approximation is coherent, so approximates some allowable $\pi$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Iterates agree on S
nodes.statement: In particular, $((\psi_{A_2}^n)_\delta)^*[S] = \pi^n[S]$ for every integer $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Powers agree with $\pi^n$ on $S$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Plan: add the orbit
nodes.statement: We intend to add the orbit $$ f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]) \mapsto f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^{n+1}(x), \pi^{n+1}[S]) $$ to $\psi_A^*$, at least up to nearness.
nodes.statement_short: Plan to add the $f$-image orbit to $\psi_A^*$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Orbit already met
nodes.statement: Suppose that there is some $n$ such that $\psi_A^*$ is defined on $f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S])$. We have $((\psi_{A_2}^n)_\delta)^*[S] = \pi^n[S]$, so $((\psi_{A_2}^{-n})_\delta)^*[\pi^n[S]] = S$. Therefore, as $\psi^{-n}$ is coherent (also by remark \ref{rk:power_deriv_coherent}), we obtain $$ (\psi^{-n})_A^* `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S). $$ Therefore, $$ f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S) \subseteq {\tt dom}(\psi_A^*).$$ So we do not need to extend $\psi$; we are already done.
nodes.statement_short: If $\psi_A^*$ meets the orbit, coherence of $\psi^{-n}$ shows nothing needs adding.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Assume orbit point in domain
nodes.statement: Suppose that there is some $n$ such that $\psi_A^*$ is defined on $f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S])$. We have $((\psi_{A_2}^n)_\delta)^*[S] = \pi^n[S]$, so $((\psi_{A_2}^{-n})_\delta)^*[\pi^n[S]] = S$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose some orbit point is in the domain.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Pull back by coherence
nodes.statement: Therefore, as $\psi^{-n}$ is coherent (also by remark \ref{rk:power_deriv_coherent}), we obtain $$ (\psi^{-n})_A^* `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S). $$ Therefore, $$ f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S) \subseteq {\tt dom}(\psi_A^*).$$
nodes.statement_short: Coherence of $\psi^{-n}$ pulls back to $f_{\delta,\gamma}(x,S)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: No extension needed
nodes.statement: So we do not need to extend $\psi$; we are already done.
nodes.statement_short: Already done.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Add the orbit
nodes.statement: Otherwise, we can extend $\psi$ to an approximation $\chi$ given by \[ \chi_A = \psi_A \cup \{ (f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]), f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^{n+1}(x), \pi^{n+1}[S])) : n \in \mathbb Z \} \] and \( \chi_B = \psi_B \) for all \( B \neq A \). It is easy to see that \( \chi \) is an extension of \( \psi \), and $$ \chi_A^* `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^{n+1}(x), \pi^{n+1}[S]) $$ for each integer $n$. Finally, we must check that this $\chi$ is coherent, but this holds by construction.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise add the whole orbit to $\psi_A$, giving a coherent extension.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Define chi
nodes.statement: Otherwise, we can extend $\psi$ to an approximation $\chi$ given by \[ \chi_A = \psi_A \cup \{ (f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]), f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^{n+1}(x), \pi^{n+1}[S])) : n \in \mathbb Z \} \] and \( \chi_B = \psi_B \) for all \( B \neq A \).
nodes.statement_short: Define $\chi_A$ by adding the orbit.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: chi extends psi
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that \( \chi \) is an extension of \( \psi \), and $$ \chi_A^* `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^n(x), \pi^n[S]) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi^{n+1}(x), \pi^{n+1}[S]) $$ for each integer $n$.
nodes.statement_short: $\chi$ extends $\psi$ and maps the orbit correctly.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Coherence by construction
nodes.statement: Finally, we must check that this $\chi$ is coherent, but this holds by construction.
nodes.statement_short: Coherence holds by construction.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: By induction, we may assume freedom of action holds at all levels $\delta < \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume freedom of action below $\beta$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Maximal extension and least undefined litter
nodes.statement: Let $\psi$ be a coherent $\beta$-approximation, and use Zorn's lemma to extend $\psi$ to a maximal coherent extension $\chi$; this step uses the fact that coherence is preserved under suprema of chains of approximations. Suppose that $\chi_A^*$ is not defined on all litters for some $A$. Let $L$ be the litter with minimal position $\iota_*(L)$ such that there is an extended type index $A$ with maximum element $\beta$ such that $L \nsubseteq {\tt dom}(\chi_A^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal coherent extension $\chi$; take the least-positioned litter on which some $\chi_A^*$ is undefined.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Flexible case
nodes.statement: Suppose that $L$ is $A$-flexible. By lemma \ref{lem:foa_flexible}, $\chi$ admits a coherent extension $\varphi$ such that $L \subseteq {\tt dom}(\varphi_A^*)$. This contradicts maximality of $\chi$.
nodes.statement_short: Flexible: lemma on flexible litters contradicts maximality.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Inflexible case
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $L$ is not $A$-flexible. Writing $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$, there are $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$ and $(x, S) \in \tau_\delta^+$ such that $L = f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S)$. We claim that $(\chi_{A_2})_\delta^*[S]$ is defined; this will then give a contradiction by lemma \ref{lem:foa_inflexible}. To show this, we must prove that if $(t, B) \in {\tt rng}(S)$, then $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined. By definition \ref{def:f_map}, we have $\iota_*^+(x, S) < \iota_*(L)$, and by (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position_constraints}}), $\iota_*(t) \leq \iota_*^+(x, S)$. If $t$ is a singleton of an atom and $t \subset M$ for a litter $M$, then by definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter}, we obtain $\iota_*(M) < \iota_*(t)$, and therefore that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined by minimality of the position of $L$. Alternatively, if $t$ is a near-litter, then if $M$ is any litter such that $M \cap t \neq \emptyset$, definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter} again implies that $\iota_*(M) \leq \iota_*(t)$, so $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``M$ is defined. Combining all such litters, we conclude that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Inflexible: the support of the coding pair is already handled, so the inflexible lemma contradicts maximality.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: L is an f-image
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $L$ is not $A$-flexible. Writing $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$, there are $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$ and $(x, S) \in \tau_\delta^+$ such that $L = f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $L=f_{\delta,\gamma}(x,S)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Claim: chi acts on S
nodes.statement: We claim that $(\chi_{A_2})_\delta^*[S]$ is defined; this will then give a contradiction by lemma \ref{lem:foa_inflexible}. To show this, we must prove that if $(t, B) \in {\tt rng}(S)$, then $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined. By definition \ref{def:f_map}, we have $\iota_*^+(x, S) < \iota_*(L)$, and by (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position_constraints}}), $\iota_*(t) \leq \iota_*^+(x, S)$. If $t$ is a singleton of an atom and $t \subset M$ for a litter $M$, then by definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter}, we obtain $\iota_*(M) < \iota_*(t)$, and therefore that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined by minimality of the position of $L$. Alternatively, if $t$ is a near-litter, then if $M$ is any litter such that $M \cap t \neq \emptyset$, definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter} again implies that $\iota_*(M) \leq \iota_*(t)$, so $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``M$ is defined. Combining all such litters, we conclude that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Claim the derived approximation is defined on $S$, contradicting maximality via the inflexible lemma.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Reduce to support conditions
nodes.statement: To show this, we must prove that if $(t, B) \in {\tt rng}(S)$, then $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to each support condition.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Position bounds
nodes.statement: By definition \ref{def:f_map}, we have $\iota_*^+(x, S) < \iota_*(L)$, and by (\textbf{I\ref{ih:position_constraints}}), $\iota_*(t) \leq \iota_*^+(x, S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Positions of support atoms and near-litters are below that of $L$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Atom case
nodes.statement: If $t$ is a singleton of an atom and $t \subset M$ for a litter $M$, then by definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter}, we obtain $\iota_*(M) < \iota_*(t)$, and therefore that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined by minimality of the position of $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Atom singletons are handled by minimality of $L$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Near-litter case
nodes.statement: Alternatively, if $t$ is a near-litter, then if $M$ is any litter such that $M \cap t \neq \emptyset$, definition \ref{def:pos_atom_near_litter} again implies that $\iota_*(M) \leq \iota_*(t)$, so $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``M$ is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Litters meeting a near-litter come earlier.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Defined on t
nodes.statement: Combining all such litters, we conclude that $(\chi_{A_2})_B^*``t$ is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Hence defined on $t$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: Conclude via total extension
nodes.statement: Therefore $\chi_A^*$ must be defined on all litters for all $A$. By remark \ref{rk:foa_suffices}, this concludes the proof: $\psi$ approximates the allowable permutation $\pi$ given by $\pi_A = \chi_A^*$.
nodes.statement_short: $\chi$ is total, so $\psi$ approximates the allowable permutation $\pi_A=\chi_A^*$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Freedom of Action theorem

nodes.name: WLOG condition (*)
nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be a coherent $\beta$-action. First, note that we may assume without loss of generality that whenever $N \in {\tt dom}(\xi_A)$, we have \begin{equation} N \Delta N^\circ \subseteq {\tt dom}(\xi_A) \ \mathrm{and}\ \xi_A(N) \Delta \xi_A(N)^\circ \subseteq {\tt rng}(\xi_A). \tag{$*$} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume WLOG condition $(*)$ on near-litters in domain and range.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Achieving (*)
nodes.statement: We can extend any $\xi$ to an action $\xi'$ with this property. If there is an atom in $N^\circ \setminus N \setminus {\tt dom}(\xi_A)$ then neither $N^{\circ}$ nor indeed any $N' \sim N$ containing the atom is in the domain of $\xi$, and we can map each such atom into an unused litter. If there is an atom in $N \setminus N^\circ \setminus {\tt dom}(\xi_A)$ then again $N^{\circ}$ is not in the domain of $\xi$ and all $N' \sim N$ which are in the domain of $\xi$ contain the atom, and we can map each such atom to an unused atom which is in $\xi_A(N)^\circ$ and also inside all $\xi_A$-images of near-litters $N' \sim N$. This handles near-litters $N$ in the domain of $\xi$; near-litters in the range of $\xi$ are handled dually. This modification preserves coherence, as it only adds images of atoms.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $\xi$ by atom images to satisfy $(*)$, preserving coherence.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Plan: build an approximation
nodes.statement: Now, we will turn $\xi$ into a $\beta$-approximation $\psi$. To do this, we need to fill in orbits of litters and atoms.
nodes.statement_short: Turn $\xi$ into an approximation by filling orbits.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Orbits of flexible litters
nodes.statement: We first show how to define orbits of flexible litters; the orbits for inflexible litters will appear automatically by coherence. For each $A$, let $g_A$ be the partial function given by $g_A(N^\circ) = \xi_A(N)^\circ$ whenever $N$ is $A$-flexible and $\xi_A(N)$ is defined; the third condition on the definition of actions ensures that this map is well-defined and injective. We define the restriction of $\psi_A$ to litters to be a small bijective extension of $g_A$, where any new litters in ${\tt dom}(\psi_A)$ are $A$-flexible and disjoint from domain and range elements of $\xi_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_A$ on litters as a small bijective extension of the induced litter map.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Orbits of atoms
nodes.statement: Next, we show how to define orbits of atoms. For each $A$, we define the restriction of $\psi_A$ to atoms to be a small bijective extension of the restriction of $\xi_A$ to atoms, with the property that $a \in N$ iff $\psi_A(a) \in \xi_A(N)$ whenever the right-hand side is defined. We now explain how to do this. Our construction proceeds in $\omega$ stages, where at each stage, we define $\psi_A$ and $\psi_A^{-1}$ at any atoms contained in the domain or range of the function defined so far. We describe the construction of images under $\psi_A$; the inverse is dual.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_A$ on atoms compatibly with membership in near-litters.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Atom restriction
nodes.statement: For each $A$, we define the restriction of $\psi_A$ to atoms to be a small bijective extension of the restriction of $\xi_A$ to atoms, with the property that $a \in N$ iff $\psi_A(a) \in \xi_A(N)$ whenever the right-hand side is defined.
nodes.statement_short: A small bijective extension of $\xi_A$ on atoms respecting membership.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Omega-stage construction
nodes.statement: We now explain how to do this. Our construction proceeds in $\omega$ stages, where at each stage, we define $\psi_A$ and $\psi_A^{-1}$ at any atoms contained in the domain or range of the function defined so far. We describe the construction of images under $\psi_A$; the inverse is dual.
nodes.statement_short: Construct in $\omega$ stages, dually for inverses.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Atom in a near-litter of the domain
nodes.statement: Suppose that we need to define $\psi_A(a)$, so in particular $a \notin {\tt dom}(\xi_A)$, and that $\xi_A(N)$ is defined for some $N \ni a$. By $(*)$, we know that $a \in N^\circ$, and additionally $a \in N'$ for every $N' \sim N$ with $N' \in {\tt dom}(\xi_A)$ because of the interference conditions. So we define $\psi_A(a)$ to be any unused atom both in $\xi_A(N)^\circ$ and also inside all $\xi_A(N')$ for $N' \sim N$. Such an atom will always exist because there are only a small amount of atoms excluded by each near-litter $N'$, and there are only a small number of such near-litters.
nodes.statement_short: Choose an unused atom inside all relevant images.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Free atom
nodes.statement: If $\xi_A(N)$ is not defined for any $N \ni a$, then we are free to choose any unused atom for $\psi_A(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise choose any unused atom.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Dual construction and smallness
nodes.statement: We perform the dual construction to define $\psi_A^{-1}$ on required atoms. When the construction concludes, the function $\psi_A$ will still be small because $\kappa$ is uncountable and regular.
nodes.statement_short: Dual construction; regularity of $\kappa$ keeps $\psi_A$ small.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Apply Freedom of Action
nodes.statement: The $\beta$-approximation $\psi$ defined as above is obviously coherent because all of the litters $L$ in the domain of $\psi_A$ are $A$-flexible, so by the Freedom of Action Theorem (\ref{thm:foa}), $\psi$ approximates some $\beta$-allowable permutation $\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi$ is coherent, so approximates an allowable $\pi$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Claim: xi approximates pi
nodes.statement: We claim that $\xi$ approximates this $\pi$. The case for atoms is obvious, so it suffices to show that for each near-litter $N$ such that $\xi_A(N)$ is defined, we have $\xi_A(N) = \pi_A `` N$. By induction we may assume that $\xi_B(M) = \pi_B `` M$ holds for all extended type indices $B$ and near-litters $M$ with $\iota_*(M) < \iota_*(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to near-litters and induct on positions.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Litters agree
nodes.statement: First, we show that $\xi_A(N)^\circ = (\pi_A `` N)^\circ$. If $N$ is $A$-flexible, we have $\xi_A(N)^\circ = \psi_A(N^\circ) = (\pi_A `` N)^\circ$ as required. Suppose instead that $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$ are such that $N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S)$ for $(x, S) \in \tau_\delta^+$. For any $(t, B)$ in the range of $S$, by coherence of $\xi$ we know that $(\xi_{A_2})_B(t)$ is defined, and moreover by inductive hypothesis, that $(\xi_{A_2})_B(t) = (\pi_{A_2})_B``t$. But this shows that $\xi_{A_2}$ agrees with $\pi_{A_2}$ on $S$, and so again by coherence, we can conclude that $$\xi_A(N) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}((\pi_{A_2})_\delta(x), (\pi_{A_2})_\delta[S]) \sim \pi_A `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S) \sim \pi_A `` N.$$
nodes.statement_short: The associated litters agree, by flexibility or by coherence.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Flexible near-litter
nodes.statement: If $N$ is $A$-flexible, we have $\xi_A(N)^\circ = \psi_A(N^\circ) = (\pi_A `` N)^\circ$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of $\psi_A$ on litters.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Inflexible near-litter
nodes.statement: Suppose instead that $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$ are such that $N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S)$ for $(x, S) \in \tau_\delta^+$.
nodes.statement_short: $N$ is near an $f$-image.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Agreement on S
nodes.statement: For any $(t, B)$ in the range of $S$, by coherence of $\xi$ we know that $(\xi_{A_2})_B(t)$ is defined, and moreover by inductive hypothesis, that $(\xi_{A_2})_B(t) = (\pi_{A_2})_B``t$.
nodes.statement_short: By induction $\xi$ and $\pi$ agree on $S$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Coherence gives nearness
nodes.statement: But this shows that $\xi_{A_2}$ agrees with $\pi_{A_2}$ on $S$, and so again by coherence, we can conclude that $$\xi_A(N) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}((\pi_{A_2})_\delta(x), (\pi_{A_2})_\delta[S]) \sim \pi_A `` f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, S) \sim \pi_A `` N.$$
nodes.statement_short: Coherence gives $\xi_A(N)\sim\pi_A``N$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Exact equality
nodes.statement: We now conclude the proof by showing that $\xi_A(N) = \pi_A `` N$. This proof depends on $(*)$, as well as the fact that the allowable permutation $\pi$ that we constructed in theorem \ref{thm:foa} has the property that for any atom $a \notin {\tt dom}(\psi)$ and any litter $L$, we have $a \in L$ if and only if $\pi(a) \in (\pi``L)^\circ$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove exact equality using $(*)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Forward inclusion
nodes.statement: Suppose that $a \in \xi_A(N)$. If $a \in {\tt rng}(\psi_A)$, then $\psi_A^{-1}(a) \in N$ by construction of $\psi_A$, but $\psi_A^{-1}(a) = \pi_A^{-1}(a)$, so $\pi_A^{-1}(a) \in N$. Otherwise, $a \in \xi_A(N)^\circ$ by $(*)$, so $\pi_A^{-1}(a) \in N^\circ$, so $\pi_A^{-1}(a) \in N$ by $(*)$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $\xi_A(N)$ lie in $\pi_A``N$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that $a \in \pi_A `` N$. If $a \in {\tt rng}(\psi_A)$, then $\pi_A^{-1}(a) = \psi_A^{-1}(a)$, so $a \in \xi_A(N)$ by construction of $\psi_A$. Otherwise, $\pi_A^{-1}(a) \in N^\circ$ by $(*)$, so $a \in (\pi_A `` N)^\circ = \xi_A(N)^\circ$, so by $(*)$ we conclude that $a \in \xi_A(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $\pi_A``N$ lie in $\xi_A(N)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits

nodes.name: Append raised supports
nodes.statement: First, for each $(x,A)$ in the range of $S$ where $\delta={\tt min}(A_1)$, $\gamma<{\tt min}(A_2)$ and $x^\circ = f_{\gamma,\delta}(y,T)$, add the range of $T^{\uparrow A_2}$ to the end of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Append raised supports of inflexible litters.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Close under the second property
nodes.statement: Repeating this process $\omega$ times, we obtain a new support $S' \supseteq S$ that satisfies the second property of being a strong support; the domain of $S'$ is still a small ordinal as $\kappa$ is uncountable and regular.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate $\omega$ times; the domain stays small.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Add interference atoms
nodes.statement: Finally, we append to $S$ all pairs $(\{z\},A)$ where $z$ is in the interference of near-litters $M,N$ where $(M,A)$, $(N,A)$ are in the range of $S$. This produces a support $S'' \supseteq S'$ which is clearly strong.
nodes.statement_short: Append interference atoms to obtain a strong support.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Specifications are invariant
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to see that if $S$ is a $\beta$-support and if $\pi$ is a $\beta$-allowable permutation, then $S^* = (\pi[S])^*$. The relationships between items in the support recorded in the specification are invariant under application of allowable permutations.
nodes.statement_short: Specifications are invariant under allowable permutations.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Remaining direction
nodes.statement: It remains to show that if $S$ and $T$ are strong supports, and $S^*=T^*$ is a specification for both, there is an allowable permutation $\pi$ such that $\pi[S]=T$.
nodes.statement_short: Show equal specifications give an allowable $\pi$ with $\pi[S]=T$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Plan: define an action
nodes.statement: We construct $\pi$ using the Freedom of Action Theorem (\ref{thm:foa_actions}). Define the $\beta$-action $\xi$ in the following way.
nodes.statement_short: Use Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits on an action $\xi$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Action on near-litters
nodes.statement: If $S_\epsilon = (M,A)$ for $M$ a near-litter, then $T_\epsilon = (N,A)$ for $N$ a near-litter, and we set $\xi_A(M) = N$. Note that if $S_\delta = (M,A)$ for some $\delta$, the fact that $S$ and $T$ have the same specification implies that $T_\delta = (N,A)$, ensuring that this is a well-defined function. Similarly, if $S_\delta = (M',A)$ and $M' \sim M$, then $T_\delta = (N',A)$ for some $N' \sim N$.
