nodes.statement_short: Send each near-litter of $S$ to the corresponding one of $T$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Action on atoms
nodes.statement: If we have $S_\epsilon = (\{x\},A)$, we will have $T_\epsilon = (\{y\},A)$ for some $y$, and so we will similarly set $\xi_A(x) = y$. Note that if $S_\delta = (\{x\},A)$, then $T_\delta = (\{y\},A)$.
nodes.statement_short: Send each atom of $S$ to the corresponding atom of $T$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: It is an action
nodes.statement: As $S$ and $T$ are strong, this description indeed defines a $\beta$-action $\xi$.
nodes.statement_short: Strength makes this a $\beta$-action.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Check flexibility clause
nodes.statement: We now check that $\xi$ is coherent. If we assigned $\xi_A(M) = N$, then $(M,A) = S_\epsilon$ and $(N,A) = T_\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon$. As $S$ and $T$ have the same specification, $M$ is $A$-flexible if and only if $N$ is $A$-flexible.
nodes.statement_short: Equal specifications preserve flexibility.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Matching positions
nodes.statement: If we assigned $\xi_A(M) = N$, then $(M,A) = S_\epsilon$ and $(N,A) = T_\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Assigned pairs occupy the same position.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Flexibility matches
nodes.statement: As $S$ and $T$ have the same specification, $M$ is $A$-flexible if and only if $N$ is $A$-flexible.
nodes.statement_short: Flexibility is recorded in the specification.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Inflexible clause
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $\xi_A(M) = N$ where $M^\circ = f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ and $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. Then $(M,A) = S_\epsilon$ and $(N,A) = T_\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon$. As $S$ and $T$ have the same specification, there is some $(y,V) \in \tau_\delta^+$ such that $N^\circ = f_{\delta,\gamma}(y,V)$ and $$ \chi_{x,U} = \chi_{y,V};\quad \{ ( \zeta, \eta ) : S_\zeta = (U^{\uparrow A_2})_\eta \} = \{ ( \zeta, \eta ) : T_\zeta = (V^{\uparrow A_2})_\eta \}. $$ Since $\chi_{x,U} = \chi_{y,V}$, there is a $\delta$-allowable permutation $\pi$ such that $\pi(x) = y$ and $\pi[U] = V$. So for any $(t,B)$ in the range of $U$, we have $S_\zeta = (t,B)$ if and only if $T_\zeta = (\pi_B(t),B)$. Therefore, as $S$ and $T$ are strong, we may conclude that $(\xi_{A_2})_\delta[U] = \pi[U]$, and that $$ \xi_A(M) = N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(y,V) = f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi(x),\pi[U]) $$ as required for coherence.
nodes.statement_short: Matching coding functions give an allowable $\pi$ realizing coherence.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Inflexible near-litter
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $\xi_A(M) = N$ where $M^\circ = f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ and $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. Then $(M,A) = S_\epsilon$ and $(N,A) = T_\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider an inflexible near-litter.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Same coding data
nodes.statement: As $S$ and $T$ have the same specification, there is some $(y,V) \in \tau_\delta^+$ such that $N^\circ = f_{\delta,\gamma}(y,V)$ and $$ \chi_{x,U} = \chi_{y,V};\quad \{ ( \zeta, \eta ) : S_\zeta = (U^{\uparrow A_2})_\eta \} = \{ ( \zeta, \eta ) : T_\zeta = (V^{\uparrow A_2})_\eta \}. $$
nodes.statement_short: The specification gives the same coding function and support positions.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Allowable permutation from coding functions
nodes.statement: Since $\chi_{x,U} = \chi_{y,V}$, there is a $\delta$-allowable permutation $\pi$ such that $\pi(x) = y$ and $\pi[U] = V$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal coding functions give $\pi$ with $\pi(x)=y$, $\pi[U]=V$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Positions correspond
nodes.statement: So for any $(t,B)$ in the range of $U$, we have $S_\zeta = (t,B)$ if and only if $T_\zeta = (\pi_B(t),B)$.
nodes.statement_short: Support conditions of $U$ correspond in $S$ and $T$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Coherence condition holds
nodes.statement: Therefore, as $S$ and $T$ are strong, we may conclude that $(\xi_{A_2})_\delta[U] = \pi[U]$, and that $$ \xi_A(M) = N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(y,V) = f_{\delta,\gamma}(\pi(x),\pi[U]) $$ as required for coherence.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the coherence condition holds.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, by the Freedom of Action Theorem (\ref{thm:foa_actions}), $\xi$ approximates some $\beta$-allowable permutation $\pi$, and in particular, $\pi$ satisfies $\pi[S] = T$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Freedom of Action gives $\pi$ with $\pi[S]=T$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Ingredients of specifications
nodes.statement: The elements of the range of a $\beta$-specification are built from finite sets of type indices below $\beta$, sets of (pairs of) elements of $\kappa$ (support domain elements), and $\gamma$-coding functions for $\gamma < \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Specifications are built from type-index sets, small ordinal data and lower coding functions.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Few finite sets of indices
nodes.statement: As $\beta < \lambda \leq \mu$, there are less than $\mu$ possible finite sets of type indices below $\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Fewer than $\mu$ finite sets of indices.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Few lower coding functions
nodes.statement: Since $\beta < \lambda \leq {\tt cf}(\mu)$, the sum of cardinals each $<\mu$ indexed by ordinals $<\beta$ will be less than $\mu$, so there are less than $\mu$ possible coding functions that can be used here.
nodes.statement_short: Cofinality bounds the lower coding functions below $\mu$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: nu to the less-than-kappa bound
nodes.statement: Hence the elements of the range of such a specification are taken from a set of size less than $\mu$, and so the cardinality of the set of specifications is bounded by $\nu^{<\kappa}$ where $\nu < \mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Specifications number at most $\nu^{<\kappa}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Strong limit
nodes.statement:
Now, $
u^{<\kappa}$ is the cardinality of the set of functions from some small ordinal to $
u$, which is less than or equal to the cardinality of the power set of $
u 	imes \kappa$, which in turn is less than $\mu$ because $\mu$ is strong limit.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu^{<\kappa}<\mu$ since $\mu$ is a strong limit.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Weak specifications
nodes.statement: For any support $S$ that is not necessarily strong, there is a suitable weaker notion of specification: give the specification for a strong support $T$ of which $S$ is an initial segment, together with the domain of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the specification of a strong extension plus the domain.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Weak specifications determine orbits
nodes.statement: These weak specifications are not unique, but they do determine the orbit in which $S$ lies in the allowable permutations.
nodes.statement_short: They determine the orbit.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Count
nodes.statement: Since there are less than $\mu$ specifications by proposition \ref{prop:count_spec}, and $\kappa < \mu$, we conclude that there are less than $\mu$ orbits in the $\beta$-supports under the allowable permutations.
nodes.statement_short: Fewer than $\mu$ orbits.
nodes.section: 4.3 Counting orbits of supports: coding functions and specifications

nodes.name: Orbits of 0-supports
nodes.statement: We describe all coding functions for type 0. The orbit of a strong 0-support in the allowable permutations is determined by the positions in the support occupied by near-litters, and for each position in the support occupied by a singleton, the positions, if any, of the near-litters in the support which include it, and for each position in the support occupied by a near-litter, the positions, if any, occupied by near-litters which are near it (this is exactly the information contained in the 0-specification of the support).
nodes.statement_short: Orbits of strong 0-supports are described by their specification.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Count orbits
nodes.statement: There are no more than $2^\kappa$ ways to specify an orbit.
nodes.statement_short: At most $2^\kappa$ orbits.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Partition of type -1
nodes.statement: Now for each such support, there is a natural partition of type $-1$ into near-litters, singletons, and a large complement set.
nodes.statement_short: A support partitions type $-1$ into near-litters, singletons and a complement.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Elements with that support
nodes.statement: The partition has $\nu<\kappa$ elements, and there are $2^\nu\leq 2^\kappa$ objects of type 0 with this support, each determined by specifying for each compartment in the partition whether it is to be included or excluded from the set.
nodes.statement_short: At most $2^\nu$ type-0 objects per support.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Bound at type 0
nodes.statement: So there are $2^\nu\leq 2^\kappa$ coding functions for that orbit in the supports, and so for any support (that need not be strong), there are at most $2^\kappa$ coding functions for its orbit, by first extending it to a strong support. So there are no more than $2^\kappa<\mu$ coding functions over type 0.
nodes.statement_short: At most $2^\kappa<\mu$ coding functions at type 0.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Type -1
nodes.statement: Any type $-1$ coding function is associated with a uniquely determined type 0 coding function of a singleton, so there are no more of the former than of the latter.
nodes.statement_short: Type $-1$ coding functions inject into type 0 ones.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Choose s
nodes.statement: Let $\chi = \chi_{x,S}$. The set we claim works is $$ s = \{ \chi_{\{y\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}} : y \in x \cap \tau_\gamma \wedge U \text{ supports } y \}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Take $s$ the raised singletons of $\gamma$-elements of $x$.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Reduce to one value
nodes.statement: Since $C_{s,\gamma} \restriction {\tt dom}(\chi)$ is a coding function, it suffices to check that $C_{s,\gamma}(S) = x$, which we show by $\gamma$-extensionality.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to check $C_{s,\gamma}(S)=x$ by $\gamma$-extensionality.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Forward inclusion
nodes.statement: If $y \in C_{s,\gamma}(S) \cap \tau_\gamma$, then there is some $z \in x \cap \tau_\gamma$, some support $U$ of $z$, and $T \supseteq S$ such that $$ y \in \chi_{\{z\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}}(T). $$ Hence there is a $\beta$-allowable $\pi$ such that $\pi[S + U^{\uparrow \beta}] = T$; in particular, $\pi[S] = S$ as $T$ is an extension of $S$, so $\pi(x) = x$. Therefore, $$ \pi_\gamma^{-1}(y) \in \chi_{\{z\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}}(\pi^{-1}[T]) = \chi_{\{z\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}}(S + U^{\uparrow \beta}) = \{z\}_\beta, $$ giving $\pi_\gamma^{-1}(y) \in x$ and so $y \in x$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of the combination lie in $x$.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $y \in x \cap \tau_\gamma$, then for any support $U$ of $y$, we immediately obtain $y \in C_{s,\gamma}(S)$ from the fact that $\chi_{\{y\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}} \in s$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $x$ lie in the combination.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: We may assume by induction that there are less than $\mu$ coding functions of every type $\gamma < \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the bound below $\beta$.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: Since the cases for $\beta = 0, -1$ were proven in lemma \ref{lem:count_coding_function_zero}, we may additionally assume that there exists some ordinal $\gamma \in \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Base cases handled; assume some $\gamma\in\beta$.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Combination form
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:eq_combine}, every $\beta$-coding function can be written in the form $C_{s,\gamma} \restriction d$, where $s$ is a set of raised $\gamma$-singletons and $d$ is an orbit of $\beta$-supports under the action of allowable permutations.
nodes.statement_short: Write coding functions as combinations of raised singletons on orbits.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Reduce to raised singletons
nodes.statement: By proposition \ref{prop:count_support_orbits}, there are less than $\mu$ such orbits, so it suffices to show there are less than $\mu$ possible sets of raised $\gamma$-singletons; indeed, as $\mu$ is a strong limit, it further suffices to simply show that there are less than $\mu$ raised $\gamma$-singletons.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to bound raised singletons.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Raised singletons are determined by few data
nodes.statement: We show that any raised singleton $\chi_{\{x\}_\beta,S + U^{\uparrow \beta}}$ is determined by ${\tt dom}(S)$, the orbit of $S + U^{\uparrow \beta}$ under the allowable permutations, and the $\gamma$-coding function $\chi_{x,U}$. Indeed, suppose that $S$ and $T$ have the same domain, $S + U^{\uparrow \beta}$ and $T + V^{\uparrow \beta}$ share the same orbit under the $\beta$-allowable permutations, and the coding functions $\chi_{x,U}$ and $\chi_{y,V}$ coincide. Then there is a $\beta$-allowable $\pi$ such that $\pi[S] = T$ and $\pi_\gamma[U] = V$, and additionally there is a $\gamma$-allowable $\pi'$ such that $\pi'[U] = V$ and $\pi'(x) = y$. Therefore, we additionally have that $\pi_\gamma(x) = y$ as $U$ supports $x$ and both $\pi_\gamma$ and $\pi'$ have the same action on $U$. Hence, the two raised singletons must coincide.
nodes.statement_short: A raised singleton is determined by a domain, an orbit and a $\gamma$-coding function.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Same data
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $S$ and $T$ have the same domain, $S + U^{\uparrow \beta}$ and $T + V^{\uparrow \beta}$ share the same orbit under the $\beta$-allowable permutations, and the coding functions $\chi_{x,U}$ and $\chi_{y,V}$ coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose the data coincide.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Permutations from data
nodes.statement: Then there is a $\beta$-allowable $\pi$ such that $\pi[S] = T$ and $\pi_\gamma[U] = V$, and additionally there is a $\gamma$-allowable $\pi'$ such that $\pi'[U] = V$ and $\pi'(x) = y$.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain allowable permutations matching the data.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Agreement at x
nodes.statement: Therefore, we additionally have that $\pi_\gamma(x) = y$ as $U$ supports $x$ and both $\pi_\gamma$ and $\pi'$ have the same action on $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Support agreement gives $\pi_\gamma(x)=y$.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Coincide
nodes.statement: Hence, the two raised singletons must coincide.
nodes.statement_short: The raised singletons coincide.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Conclude count
nodes.statement: It now simply remains to note that there are less than $\mu$ such orbits of $\beta$-supports under the allowable permutations by proposition \ref{prop:count_support_orbits}, and that we assume by inductive hypothesis that there are less than $\mu$ coding functions of type $\gamma$, in order to conclude the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Fewer than $\mu$ orbits and lower coding functions give the bound.
nodes.section: 4.4 Types are of size $\mu$ (because there are $<\mu$ coding functions per type)

nodes.name: Membership relation E
nodes.statement: Use $E$ for the membership relation $\in_{TTT}$ of the structure defined above (in which the membership of type $\beta$ objects in type $\alpha$ objects is actually a subrelation of the membership relation of the metatheory, a fact inherited from the scheme of supertypes).
nodes.statement_short: Let $E$ be the model's membership.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Invariance of membership
nodes.statement: It should be evident that $x E y \leftrightarrow \pi_\beta(x) E \pi(y)$, where $x$ is of type $\beta$, $y$ is of type $\alpha$, and $\pi$ is an $\alpha$-allowable permutation.
nodes.statement_short: Membership is invariant under allowable permutations.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Set up comprehension instance
nodes.statement: Suppose that we are considering the existence of $\{x : \phi^s\}$, where $\phi$ is a formula of the language of TST with $\in$ translated as $E$, and $s$ is a strictly increasing sequence of types\footnote{We use notation $s(i)$ instead of $s_i$ to avoid undue nesting of subscripts, in what follows.}. Note that the TTT type of $x$ is some $s(j)$ and the TTT type of $\{x : \phi^s\}$ is $s(j+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider a translated comprehension instance.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Truth preserved
nodes.statement: For any $s(j+1)$-allowable permutation $\pi$, the truth value of each subformula of $\phi$ will be preserved if we replace each $u$ of type $s(i)$ with $\pi_{A_{s,i}}(u)$, where $A_{s,i}$ is the set of all $s(k)$ for $i \leq k \leq j+1$ [there being no variables of type higher than $s(j+1)$]: $\pi_{A_{s,i}}(x) E \pi_{A_{s,i+1}}(y)$ is equivalent to $(\pi_{A_{s,i+1}})_{s(i)}(x) E \pi_{A_{s,i+1}}(y)$, which is equivalent to $xEy$ by the observation above.
nodes.statement_short: Applying derivatives preserves truth of subformulas.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Parameters fixed
nodes.statement: The formula $\phi$ will contain various parameters $a_i$ of types $s(n_i)$ and it is then evident that the set $\{x : \phi^s\}$ will be fixed by any $s(j+1)$-allowable permutation $\pi$ such that $\pi_{A_{s,n_i}}$ fixes $a_i$ for each $i$.
nodes.statement_short: The set is fixed by permutations fixing the parameters.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Set is symmetric
nodes.statement: But this means that $\{x : \phi^s\}_{s(j+1)}$ is symmetric and belongs to type $s(j+1)$: we can merge the supports of the $a_i$'s (with suitable raising of indices) into a single $s(j+1)$-support.
nodes.statement_short: Merging parameter supports shows the set is symmetric, hence in the type.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Where predicativity was used
nodes.statement: Notice that we assumed the predicativity condition that no variable more than one type higher than $x$ appears (in the sense of TST).
nodes.statement_short: Predicativity was used here.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Scope
nodes.statement: This procedure will certainly work if the set definition is predicative (all bound variables are of type no higher than that of $x$, parameters at the type of the set being defined are allowed), but it also works for some impredicative set definitions.
nodes.statement_short: Works for predicative and some impredicative definitions.
nodes.section: 4.5 The structure is a model of predicative TTT

nodes.name: Strong support
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\{\{g\}_\beta:g \in G\}_\alpha$ is symmetric. It then has a strong support $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a strong support $S$ of the set of singletons.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Claim: restricted support
nodes.statement: We claim that $S_{(\beta)}$, defined as $\{(z,C): {\tt max}(C)=\beta \wedge (z,C\cup \{\alpha\}) \in S\}$, is a $\beta$-support for $G_\beta$, where without loss of generality we assume that $S$ has been reordered such that the domain of $S_{(\beta)}$ (and $(S_{(\beta)})_{(\gamma)}$) is an ordinal.
nodes.statement_short: Claim that the restriction $S_{(\beta)}$ supports $G_\beta$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Support of g
nodes.statement: Any $g \in G$ has a strong $\gamma$-support $T$ which extends $(S_{(\beta)})_{(\gamma)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a strong support $T$ of $g$ extending the restriction.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Permutation fixing restriction
nodes.statement: Suppose that the action of a $\beta$-allowable permutation $\pi$ fixes $S_{(\beta)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\pi$ fix $S_{(\beta)}$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Our plan is to use Freedom of Action technology to construct an $\alpha$-allowable permutation $\pi^*$ whose action on $S$ is the identity and whose action on $T^{\uparrow\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ precisely parallels the action of $\pi$ on $T^{\uparrow\beta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\pi^*$ fixing $S$ and copying $\pi$ on $T$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Plan suffices
nodes.statement: If this is accomplished, then the action of $\pi^*$ fixes $S$ and so fixes $$\{\{g\}_\beta:g \in G\}_\alpha,$$ while at the same time $(\pi^*_\beta)_\gamma$ agrees with $\pi_\gamma$ at $g$. This implies that $$ \pi_\gamma(g) = (\pi^*_\beta)_\gamma(g) \in (\pi^*_\beta)_\gamma `` G = G. $$ The same construction can be done for $\pi^{-1}$ in place of $\pi$ (for each $g$), so $\pi$ fixes $G_\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Such $\pi^*$ shows $\pi$ maps $G$ into itself; with $\pi^{-1}$, $\pi$ fixes $G_\beta$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Define the action
nodes.statement: We construct the allowable permutation $\pi^*$ by the Freedom of Action Theorem (\ref{thm:foa_actions}), by defining the following $\alpha$-action $\xi$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Freedom of Action for incomplete orbits on an $\alpha$-action $\xi$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Action on S and T*
nodes.statement: For every $(\{x\},A) \in {\tt rng}(S)$, we define $\xi_A(x) = x$, and for every $(N,A) \in {\tt rng}(S)$ for $N$ a near-litter, we define $\xi_A(N) = N$. Extend $T^{\uparrow\beta}$ to a strong $\beta$-support $T^*$ {(as in proposition \ref{prop:extend_to_strong_support})}, then if $(\{x\},B) \in {\tt rng}(T^*)$, we define $(\xi_\beta)_B(x) = \pi_B(x)$, and if $(N,B) \in {\tt rng}(T^*)$ for $N$ a near-litter, we similarly define $(\xi_\beta)_B(N) = \pi_B(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identity on $S$, $\pi$ on a strong extension $T^*$ of $T$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Reduce to coherence
nodes.statement: It now suffices to check that this action is coherent; then, by the Freedom of Action Theorem, we will obtain $\pi^*$ with the property that $\pi^*[S] = S$ and $\pi^*_\beta[T^*] = \pi[T^*]$, so in particular, $(\pi^*_\beta)_\gamma[T] = \pi_\gamma[T]$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to check coherence.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Two cases
nodes.statement: If $\xi_A(N)$ is defined, we have two cases: either $(N,A)$ appears in $S$, in which case $\xi_A(N) = N$, or $B = A\setminus\{\alpha\}$ has maximum element $\beta$ and $(N,B)$ occurs in $T^*$ with $\xi_A(N) = \pi_B(N)$. Note that if both of these cases are true at the same time, then as $\pi$ fixes $S_{(\beta)}$, the two defined images of $N$ coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Near-litters come from $S$ or from $T^*$; the images agree when both.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Case S
nodes.statement: In the first case, the case for flexibility is trivial, and if $N \sim f_{\delta,{\tt min}(A_1)}(x,U)$ with $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$, then as $S$ is a strong support, the range of $U^{\uparrow A_2}$ is a subset of the range of $S$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Strength of $S$ gives coherence.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Case T*
nodes.statement: We now consider the second case. If $N$ is $A$-flexible, we claim that $\pi_B(N)$ is also $A$-flexible. Suppose that $\pi_B(N) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ for $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. Then by the coherence condition, assuming $B$ has length at least 3, $$ N \sim \pi_B^{-1}``f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}((\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta(x), (\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta[U]), $$ so $N$ is $A$-inflexible, giving a contradiction. In the case that $B$ does not have length at least 3, it must have length exactly 2 because $A$ has length at least 3, so we have $A = \{ \alpha, \beta, -1 \}$ and $B = \{ \beta, -1 \}$. Note that $(N, B)$ occurs in $T^*$, so it either came from a support condition in $T$, which is impossible as $B = \{ \beta, -1 \}$ does not contain $\gamma$, or it came from a type-raised copy of an $\eta$-support we needed to include in $T^*$ to make it a strong support. But $\eta \neq -1$ as $-1$-supports cannot contain near-litter support conditions, and if $\eta$ were a proper type index, we would have $-1 < \eta < \beta$ and $\eta \in B$, also giving a contradiction. Finally, suppose that $N$ is $A$-inflexible, so $N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ for $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. By the argument of the previous paragraph, we must conclude that $A$ is of length at least 4, and so $\gamma = {\tt min}(B_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(B_2)$. As $T^*$ is strong, it contains a suitably type-raised copy of $U$, and so we are done by definition of the action of $\xi$ on $T^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Coherence for near-litters from $T^*$.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Flexible near-litter
nodes.statement: If $N$ is $A$-flexible, we claim that $\pi_B(N)$ is also $A$-flexible. Suppose that $\pi_B(N) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ for $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. Then by the coherence condition, assuming $B$ has length at least 3, $$ N \sim \pi_B^{-1}``f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}((\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta(x), (\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta[U]), $$ so $N$ is $A$-inflexible, giving a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Flexibility is preserved.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Assume image inflexible
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi_B(N) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ for $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose the image is inflexible.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Then by the coherence condition, assuming $B$ has length at least 3, $$ N \sim \pi_B^{-1}``f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U) \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}((\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta(x), (\pi_{B_2}^{-1})_\delta[U]), $$ so $N$ is $A$-inflexible, giving a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Coherence makes $N$ inflexible, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Short B
nodes.statement: In the case that $B$ does not have length at least 3, it must have length exactly 2 because $A$ has length at least 3, so we have $A = \{ \alpha, \beta, -1 \}$ and $B = \{ \beta, -1 \}$. Note that $(N, B)$ occurs in $T^*$, so it either came from a support condition in $T$, which is impossible as $B = \{ \beta, -1 \}$ does not contain $\gamma$, or it came from a type-raised copy of an $\eta$-support we needed to include in $T^*$ to make it a strong support. But $\eta \neq -1$ as $-1$-supports cannot contain near-litter support conditions, and if $\eta$ were a proper type index, we would have $-1 < \eta < \beta$ and $\eta \in B$, also giving a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: The length-2 case cannot occur.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Inflexible near-litter
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose that $N$ is $A$-inflexible, so $N \sim f_{\delta,\gamma}(x, U)$ for $\gamma = {\tt min}(A_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(A_2)$. By the argument of the previous paragraph, we must conclude that $A$ is of length at least 4, and so $\gamma = {\tt min}(B_1)$ and $\delta < {\tt min}(B_2)$. As $T^*$ is strong, it contains a suitably type-raised copy of $U$, and so we are done by definition of the action of $\xi$ on $T^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Strength of $T^*$ gives coherence.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Induction on formulas
nodes.statement: What we need to do is verify that $\{x:\phi\}$ exists for each formula $\phi$ of the language of TST, to ensure that comprehension holds. We do this by induction on the structure of formulas.
nodes.statement_short: Verify comprehension by induction on formulas.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Negation
nodes.statement: $\{x:\neg \phi\}$ is $\{x :\phi\}^c$.
nodes.statement_short: Negation by complement.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Conjunction
nodes.statement: $\{x :\phi \wedge \psi\}$ is $\{x:\phi \} \cap \{x:\psi\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjunction by intersection.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Quantifier case
nodes.statement: Now we have the much more complex task of analyzing $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}.$$ Choose a type $\tau'$ higher than the type $\tau_i$ of each $t_i$. Do this for bound variables as well, and further, in each formula $(\forall t_i:\psi)$ or $(\exists t_i:\psi)$ we require that all occurrences of $t_i$ be free in $\psi$ and the index of $t_i$ be less than the index of any other variable appearing free in $\psi$. It should be clear that we can do this without loss of generality. Where the type of $t_i$ is $\tau_i$, we define $x_i$ as $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)$: we construct $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}$$ by defining manipulations which allow us to build sets $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):\phi^*(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\}$ in which all the variables are of the same type. We write $\phi^*$ to suggest that the formula $\phi$ must be transformed to effect our change of variables: $t_i = t_j$ is equivalent to $x_i = x_j$, and $t_i \in t_j$ is equivalent to $(x_i,x_j) \in [\in]^{\iota^{\tau'-\tau_j}}$ (the reader will see that we use this representation below, though embedded in larger tuples). A quantifier over $t_i$ is equivalent to a quantifier over $x_i$ restricted to $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}``V$. For any such representation, we have a type signature $$\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}``V \times \ldots \times \iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}``V.$$ We abbreviate this as $\tau^*$. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_1 = x_n\}$ is obtained as $I_{2,2}^{n-2}(\iota^2``V)\cap \tau^*$. The set $\{(x_1,\dots,x_n):x_1 = x_i\}$ ($i<n$) is obtained as $I_{2,3}^{i-2}(I_3(\iota^2``V))\cap \tau^*$. We then can represent the set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = x_j\}$ (wlog $i<j$) as \newline $I_{1,n-i+1}^{i-1}(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-i+1}):x_1 = x_{j-i+1}\})\cap \tau^*$. The set $\{(\{x_1\},x_2):x_1 \in x_2\}$ has already been defined above as $[\in]$. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists uv:x_i = \iota^{k+1}(u) \wedge x_j = \iota^k(v) \wedge u\in v)\}$ is $${\tt rng}^2(I_3(R^{\iota^{k+2n}}[\in]) \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_1 = x_{i+2}\} \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_2=x_{j+2}\}).$$ This handles all representations of membership statements between $x_i$'s in the framework we are using. The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists x_1:(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in R)\}$ is representable as $I_{1,n-1}({\tt rng}(R))$. This only allows us to quantify over the lowest numbered variable. This is actually sufficient. We have renamed bound variables so that all bound variables with different binders are distinct and in any subformula $(\exists y:\psi)$ $y$ will have lower index than any variable free in $\psi$. Then the quantified variable might not be $x_1$, but if it is $x_k$, we can use the representation $I^{k}_{1,n-k}({\tt rng}^k(R))$: strip off the first $k-1$ variables, which are dummies already quantified over, quantify over $x_k$ (stripping off one more variable) and put $k$ dummies back, as it were. This gives sufficient machinery to handle representations of all sentences in the language of TST (or stratified sentences in the language of NF) in the format we are using. However, the final representation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ obtained in this way will be of the form $R=\{(\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}(t_1),\ldots,\iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}(t_n)):\phi(t_1.\ldots,t_n)\}$ where some of the $t_i$'s are bound variables (all values of which will appear), and some are parameters. Let $P$ be the set of $i$ such that $t_i$ is a parameter. The final computation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ will be as $$\iota^{-(\tau'-\tau_{n})}``\left({\tt rng}^{n-1}\left(R \cap \bigcap_{i \in P}\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = \iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)\}\right)\right)$$ where a final bit of computation must be exhibited: $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = t\}$ is realized as $I^{i-1}_{1,2}(\{\iota^{2(n-i-1)}(t)\}\times V)\cap \tau^*.$
nodes.statement_short: The quantifier case.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: State the task
nodes.statement: Now we have the much more complex task of analyzing $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Analyze sets defined by quantified formulas.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Normalize variables
nodes.statement: Choose a type $\tau'$ higher than the type $\tau_i$ of each $t_i$. Do this for bound variables as well, and further, in each formula $(\forall t_i:\psi)$ or $(\exists t_i:\psi)$ we require that all occurrences of $t_i$ be free in $\psi$ and the index of $t_i$ be less than the index of any other variable appearing free in $\psi$. It should be clear that we can do this without loss of generality.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a top type and order variables WLOG.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Lift to a common type
nodes.statement: Where the type of $t_i$ is $\tau_i$, we define $x_i$ as $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)$: we construct $$\{t_{n}:(\forall t_i:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n))\}$$ by defining manipulations which allow us to build sets $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):\phi^*(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\}$ in which all the variables are of the same type. We write $\phi^*$ to suggest that the formula $\phi$ must be transformed to effect our change of variables: $t_i = t_j$ is equivalent to $x_i = x_j$, and $t_i \in t_j$ is equivalent to $(x_i,x_j) \in [\in]^{\iota^{\tau'-\tau_j}}$ (the reader will see that we use this representation below, though embedded in larger tuples). A quantifier over $t_i$ is equivalent to a quantifier over $x_i$ restricted to $\iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}``V$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace variables by iterated singletons of one type.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Type signature
nodes.statement: For any such representation, we have a type signature $$\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}``V \times \ldots \times \iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}``V.$$ We abbreviate this as $\tau^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the signature $\tau^*$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Equality of first and last
nodes.statement: The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_1 = x_n\}$ is obtained as $I_{2,2}^{n-2}(\iota^2``V)\cap \tau^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $x_1=x_n$ with insertion two.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Equality of first and i-th
nodes.statement: The set $\{(x_1,\dots,x_n):x_1 = x_i\}$ ($i<n$) is obtained as $I_{2,3}^{i-2}(I_3(\iota^2``V))\cap \tau^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $x_1=x_i$ with insertion two and three.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: General equality
nodes.statement: We then can represent the set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = x_j\}$ (wlog $i<j$) as \newline $I_{1,n-i+1}^{i-1}(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-i+1}):x_1 = x_{j-i+1}\})\cap \tau^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $x_i=x_j$ with insertion one.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Membership relation
nodes.statement: The set $\{(\{x_1\},x_2):x_1 \in x_2\}$ has already been defined above as $[\in]$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $[\in]$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Membership between variables
nodes.statement: The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists uv:x_i = \iota^{k+1}(u) \wedge x_j = \iota^k(v) \wedge u\in v)\}$ is $${\tt rng}^2(I_3(R^{\iota^{k+2n}}[\in]) \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_1 = x_{i+2}\} \cap \{(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+2}):x_2=x_{j+2}\}).$$ This handles all representations of membership statements between $x_i$'s in the framework we are using.
nodes.statement_short: Express membership via ranges of insertions of $[\in]$.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Existential quantifier
nodes.statement: The set $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):(\exists x_1:(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in R)\}$ is representable as $I_{1,n-1}({\tt rng}(R))$.
nodes.statement_short: Quantify the first variable using range and insertion one.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Quantifying other variables
nodes.statement: This only allows us to quantify over the lowest numbered variable. This is actually sufficient. We have renamed bound variables so that all bound variables with different binders are distinct and in any subformula $(\exists y:\psi)$ $y$ will have lower index than any variable free in $\psi$. Then the quantified variable might not be $x_1$, but if it is $x_k$, we can use the representation $I^{k}_{1,n-k}({\tt rng}^k(R))$: strip off the first $k-1$ variables, which are dummies already quantified over, quantify over $x_k$ (stripping off one more variable) and put $k$ dummies back, as it were.
nodes.statement_short: Renaming lets every quantifier act on the lowest index.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Parameters
nodes.statement: This gives sufficient machinery to handle representations of all sentences in the language of TST (or stratified sentences in the language of NF) in the format we are using. However, the final representation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ obtained in this way will be of the form $R=\{(\iota^{\tau'-\tau_1}(t_1),\ldots,\iota^{\tau'-\tau_n}(t_n)):\phi(t_1.\ldots,t_n)\}$ where some of the $t_i$'s are bound variables (all values of which will appear), and some are parameters. Let $P$ be the set of $i$ such that $t_i$ is a parameter.
nodes.statement_short: All sentences are representable; parameters remain.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Final computation
nodes.statement: The final computation of $\{t_n:\phi(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\}$ will be as $$\iota^{-(\tau'-\tau_{n})}``\left({\tt rng}^{n-1}\left(R \cap \bigcap_{i \in P}\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = \iota^{\tau'-\tau_i}(t_i)\}\right)\right)$$ where a final bit of computation must be exhibited: $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i = t\}$ is realized as $I^{i-1}_{1,2}(\{\iota^{2(n-i-1)}(t)\}\times V)\cap \tau^*.$
nodes.statement_short: Fix parameters, take ranges and lower by inverse singleton images.
nodes.section: 2.4 An axiomatization of TST with finitely many templates

nodes.name: Countable descending witness
nodes.statement: The reason is that in the metatheory any linear order which is not a well-ordering admits a countable set with no minimal element (the range of a strictly decreasing sequence). This requires choice, but choice holds in the metatheory.
nodes.statement_short: A non-well-ordering has a countable subset without least element (using metatheoretic choice).
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Countable completeness
nodes.statement: So, if a relation represented in the model of TTT is not a well-ordering from the standpoint of the metatheory, there is a countable subcollection of its domain which has no minimal element, and this countable subset is actually realized in the model of TTT, because our models of TTT are countably complete, so the model of TTT sees that the relation is not a well-ordering.
nodes.statement_short: Countable completeness puts the witness in the model.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Supported well-ordering
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a set in a model of TTT constructed by our method which admits a well-ordering (defined along a particular type sequence). The well-ordering $\leq_X$ of $X$ which we are given must have a support.
nodes.statement_short: The given well-ordering of $X$ has a support.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: Common support
nodes.statement: A permutation which fixes the support of $\leq_X$ [in the appropriate sense defined in the paper] will fix $\leq_X$ and, because $\leq_X$ is a well-ordering in the sense of the metatheory, its action on the type of the elements of $X$ (in the type sequence with respect to which $\leq_X$ is a well-ordering) must fix each element of $X$, so in fact we have a common support for all elements of $X$, which in turn gives a support for each subcollection of $X$ in the sense of the metatheory as implemented in the appropriate type in the particular type sequence, so all of these are sets in the model of TTT (in the appropriate type in the particular type sequence) and further gives a support for the well-ordering of the power set of $X$ induced by any well-ordering of the power set of $X$ in the sense of the metatheory, so the power set of $X$ is well-ordered in the model of TTT.
nodes.statement_short: Permutations fixing it fix every element of $X$, so all subsets and a well-ordering of the power set are supported.
nodes.section: 5.2 Questions and a result about global choice-like statements

nodes.name: NF with Counting
nodes.statement: Our methods show the existence of a model of NF with the Axiom of Counting.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain NF + Counting.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Transfer to TST and bounded Zermelo
nodes.statement: This gives us a model of TST in which the Specker tree of some cardinal is of infinite rank. It is straightforward to produce a model of bounded Zermelo set theory either with atoms or with extensionality and failure of foundation from a model of TST, which will satisfy the same stratified sentences: identify the elements of type 0 either as atoms or with their own singletons, then implement elements of each type $i+1$ as subsets of type $i$ as guided by the original model of TST, identifying type $i+1$ objects with elements of lower types which have been assigned the same extension.
nodes.statement_short: Get a TST model with an infinite-rank Specker tree and convert it to bounded Zermelo.
nodes.section: 5.4 Some esoteric questions answered

nodes.name: Remaining: union
nodes.statement: What remains to complete the proof is that typed versions of the axiom of set union hold. That this is sufficient is a fact about predicative type theory.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to verify typed union; sufficiency is a fact about predicative type theory.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Iterated singletons
nodes.statement: If we have predicative comprehension and union, we note that for any formula $\phi$, $\{\iota^k(x):\phi(x)\}$ will be predicative if $k$ is taken to be large enough, then application of union $k$ times to this set will give $\{x:\phi(x)\}$. $\iota(x)$ here denotes $\{x\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Unions of predicative sets of iterated singletons give any set.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union

nodes.name: Reduce to singletons
nodes.statement: It is evidently sufficient to prove that unions of sets of singletons exist.
nodes.statement_short: So unions of sets of singletons suffice.
nodes.section: 4.6 Impredicativity: verifying the axiom of union
